articles.title: WhatsApp ocultará por defecto el número de teléfono y cada usuario escogerá quién lo puede ver
articles.text:
WhatsApp prepara un cambio en su política de privacidad que afectará a millones de usuarios que utilizan nombres de usuario en la aplicación. La plataforma trabaja para que cada persona decida quién puede ver su número de teléfono, y todo indica que la opción “Nadie” será la predeterminada para las cuentas con alias.
El hallazgo corresponde a una función todavía en desarrollo, detectada por WABetaInfo en la versión beta para Android, disponible en Google Play Store. No se trata de un despliegue activo, sino de un ajuste en construcción dentro de la sección de privacidad de la aplicación.
Cuatro opciones para decidir quién ve el número en WhatsApp
El nuevo apartado se ubicaría junto a los controles que ya existen para gestionar datos como la última conexión o la foto de perfil. Desde allí, cada usuario podrá elegir entre cuatro niveles de visibilidad para su número telefónico en llamadas y conversaciones.
Las opciones previstas son: Todos, Mis contactos, Mis contactos excepto y Nadie. Esta última quedará activada de forma automática para las cuentas que tengan configurado un nombre de usuario, sin que haga falta modificar nada para mantener el número oculto.
La función responde a la necesidad de permitir que alguien sea localizable por su alias sin exponer su número a desconocidos. Es una herramienta de privacidad que, en su versión predeterminada, mantiene oculto el dato personal mientras conserva la posibilidad de contacto a través del nombre elegido.
Una novedad en la que WhatsApp ya venía trabajando
Esta novedad se apoya en otra función que WhatsApp ya había incorporado: el campo de nombre de usuario en la pantalla de creación de contactos, identificado en la actualización beta 2.26.31.2 para Android. Ese cambio permite guardar a un contacto a partir de su alias en lugar de su número.
Cuando alguien configura un nombre de usuario, WhatsApp oculta de forma predeterminada su número ante quienes no lo tienen guardado en la agenda. En concreto, si una persona inicia una conversación con otra a través de su alias, no podrá ver su número telefónico.
El nuevo sistema de cuatro opciones no modifica ese comportamiento de base, que seguirá siendo el estándar para cualquiera que use un nombre de usuario. Lo que aporta es la posibilidad de ampliar esa visibilidad si el usuario decide compartir el número con ciertos contactos o con todo el mundo.
Hay motivos por los que alguien podría querer mostrar su número pese a tener un alias. Algunos buscan ser localizables por nombre de usuario mientras mantienen el número visible para sus contactos guardados. Otros prefieren excluir a personas puntuales de esa visibilidad sin cerrarla al resto.
Qué pasa con quienes ya conocen el número
Una de las limitaciones del nuevo control es que no borra información ya existente. Las personas que ya conocen el número de un usuario seguirán viéndolo, aunque este elija la opción “Nadie” en el nuevo ajuste.
Esto significa que la herramienta no actúa de manera retroactiva sobre contactos previos. Su función es regular la visibilidad hacia adelante, para quienes todavía no tienen ese dato guardado o para quienes el usuario quiera excluir de forma expresa.
La interfaz en desarrollo incluye además una advertencia al momento de cambiar de configuración. Cuando alguien modifica su opción de privacidad, WhatsApp restablece la lista de excepciones previamente configurada, según detalló WABetaInfo.
Esto implica que algunas personas que habían sido excluidas bajo la opción “Mis contactos excepto” podrían recuperar la visibilidad del número si el usuario cambia después a otra configuración. La aplicación presentará un cuadro de confirmación antes de aplicar el cambio, para que quede claro que la visibilidad del número se modificará.
Cuándo llega esta función
El desarrollo se encuentra, por ahora, únicamente en fase de pruebas dentro del programa beta para Android. Aunque la función ya puede detectarse en el código de la aplicación, todavía no está disponible para probarse de forma activa.
WhatsApp no ha comunicado cuándo habilitará este ajuste para los participantes del programa beta ni en qué momento llegará a la versión pública de la aplicación.

articles.title: I tested the iPhone 18 Pro's variable aperture and new Photographic Styles in New Zealand — here are 35 of my favorite photos
articles.text:
I took the iPhone 18 Pro to New Zealand to find out just how good its cameras really are — here are 35 of my favorite photos, and the settings I used to capture them
The 18 Pro is a step forward for iPhone photography — but is it a shuffle or a leap? The answer is complicated.
Apple has touted the addition of a variable aperture main camera on the new iPhone 18 Pro, claiming it delivers an improvement in low-light photos and video, and more control over depth of field when composing shots.
But with an almost identical design and spec sheet to the excellent iPhone 17 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro begs the question: are these camera upgrades incremental, or worth the extra investment?
I received my iPhone 18 Pro review sample on September 21, two days before flying to New Zealand for a month-long trip to see family and friends. The country's dramatic scenery proved the perfect place to put the iPhone 18 Pro through its paces, and I ended up shooting more than 750 still images to see if Apple's much-hyped photography upgrades cut the mustard.
In addition to that variable aperture feature, Apple also added ‘pro’ manual controls to the iPhone 18 Pro's camera app for the first time, as well as more customization options for Photographic Styles, including a film effect and film grain effect.
Cumulatively, these granular control options are quite un-Apple, putting much more control in the hands of an iPhone photographer who might be used to a simpler point-and-shoot experience.
In doing so, Apple is asking for its latest iPhone to be held to a higher standard. And the bottom line is that, while the iPhone 18 Pro has the best and most versatile camera setup of any iPhone to date, there are more capable alternatives available just a short hop over the tech fence in Android land for platform-agnostic mobile photographers who want the very best available.
Variable aperture
The variable aperture is a physically moving mechanism that can be manually changed between four different f-stops — the smaller the f-stop number, the more light is allowed to reach the lens, and vice versa.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The iPhone 18 Pro’s main camera is a 48MP sensor that can switch between f/1.4, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0. This makes it the most flexible iPhone camera lens to date, but Apple only allows those four settings — unlike a real camera, you can’t adjust to incremental f-stops between those numbers.
Changing the aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro subtly changes how much background blur a shot has when there's a subject in focus in the foreground. This is how cameras work, but usually, the small sensor on a phone requires software-enabled portrait modes to achieve this bokeh effect.
The iPhone 18 Pro can do it with hardware only, though the difference between the four settings is quite minimal, as seen here:
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
You can change the aperture manually, but it’ll also change automatically by default. And after a month of using the iPhone 18 Pro as my main camera, I feel this is still how Apple's latest flagship should be used: as a point-and-shoot camera with its default settings enabled. As you can see from many of my favorite images, the iPhone chooses the main lens at f/1.8 frequently, and it'll usually be spot on.
As mentioned, this variable aperture is the headline feature of the iPhone 18 Pro, but the subtlety with which it changes the photography experience versus the iPhone 17 Pro suggests there’s not much more Apple can do with its flagship camera system.
That said, the addition of customizable ‘pro’ controls within the camera app is a nice touch. I set my control panel to show shutter speed, white balance, and aperture, and they were fun to play around with to achieve better shots in low light, for instance. But unless you're invested in wringing the best possible results from the iPhone 18 Pro's lenses, you’ll likely forget about these new controls after a while.
The good news is that, if you're a more casual shooter, Tap to Focus continues to work well on the iPhone 18 Pro. I was impressed with the main lens' ability to capture the two images below. Tapping on the background and foreground, respectively, quickly focused on the part of the scene I wanted to highlight, with strong results.
I’ve managed shots like this on phones like the Xiaomi 17 Ultra, but that handset has a much larger 1-inch sensor. It's a testament to Apple's hardware and software prowess that the iPhone 18 Pro’s smaller 1/1.28" sensor can be this capable.
Android phones have long had more technically capable camera systems than iPhones, and while that is still the case, the iPhone 18 Pro represents yet another small shuffle forward for Apple.
Photographic Styles
Apple has also updated the Photographic Styles on offer for the iPhone 18 Pro, and they're much more varied than before.
Below, I've included the same shot taken in succession with several different filters (in their default setting) applied, and noted each filter name in the caption. To my eye, some are tastefully done, others less so:
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Handily, if you don't love the look of a particular filter, you can dive into each one and tweak both ‘palette’ and ‘texture’ granularly (though the little dot matrix Apple offers to do this is fiddly, and doesn't explain what you're actually changing).
Within ‘texture’, you can add a film effect and then even extra film grain over that. It’s a bit heavy-handed for my liking, but I did get some cool shots from it:
4x telephoto
While Apple has advertised the variable aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro's main lens more than any other feature, I still really enjoy shooting with its 48MP 4x optical telephoto lens, which has no such capability.
It's the best-looking telephoto I’ve used on an iPhone to date, with optical image stabilization resulting in crisp and well-rendered shots. Some of these were captured on the move while pushing a pram, so a hat tip to the iPhone's ability to eliminate blur (or my steady hands — you decide).
All were taken in the iPhone 18 Pro's default shooting mode, with the Standard filter:
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Admittedly, this telephoto lens is still not as capable as those you'll find on phones like the Xiaomi 17 Ultra, which boasts a formidable 200MP sensor and continuous optical zoom, or the Vivo X300 Ultra, whose own 200MP lens offers exceptional detail and tone. But it is stellar for an iPhone, and that's notable given Apple has long lagged behind the Android competition when it comes to imaging performance.
It's significant, too, that these small hardware improvements are paired with Apple's excellent iOS software. I love the Vivo X300 Ultra’s camera, but I find it hard to enjoy using Vivo phones for long periods given their comparatively unpolished Android software. Apple continues to rank at the top of the pile for software slickness.
Verdict
This was the first time I’d tested a Pro iPhone for an extended period of time since the iPhone 15 Pro Max, and compared to that phone, the 18 Pro feels like a sizable step forward in both hardware and software.
But that's a three-year evolution that I’ve been able to experience. The 18 Pro is certainly only a tiny step forward versus the 17 Pro, and it's not too far ahead of the 16 Pro, either.
So for iPhone fans who want a substantial camera upgrade over their current device, I'd only recommend upgrading to the iPhone 18 Pro if you've got an iPhone 15 Pro or older. You’ll certainly notice the step up in overall quality.
And although Apple sings the praises of the 18 Pro’s variable aperture feature in its wall-to-wall marketing of its new phone, in truth, it’s the cumulative effect of several years of iteration that make an iPhone’s camera system feel like a true upgrade.
That's the best praise I can give these excellent cameras, along with the simple fact that they're incredibly fun to shoot with, which I haven't always found while reviewing iPhones over the past decade.
To finish, here are some more of my favorite New Zealand-shot photos that I feel showcase the iPhone 18 Pro's versatility:
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Android die-hard pixel peepers will understandably stick to their superior hardware. But as far as iPhones go, the 18 Pro will surely please all who carry it as their main camera.

articles.title: Un airfryer équipé d’une caméra regarde directement ce que vous mettez dans son panier puis l'IA sélectionne seule la température et le temps de cuisson
articles.text:
Un airfryer équipé d’une caméra regarde directement ce que vous mettez dans son panier puis l'IA sélectionne seule la température et le temps de cuisson
L'IA s'invite partout, jusque dans un airfryer avec le Severin S-Fry Digital AI. Ce modèle a la particularité d'intégrer une IA qui regarde directement les aliments dans le panier, puis ensuite Food Detect Pro choisit le programme avec la température et la durée de cuisson. Prix : 169,90 €.
Le principe du Severin S-Fry Digital AI est très simple. La caméra est située au-dessus du panier et analyse le contenu quand le mode automatique est lancé. L'IA s'occupe de reconnaître la nourriture et sa quantité, puis de sélectionner l'un des programmes enregistrés.
Un airfryer avec IA qui s'occupe de tout
Exit le fait d'appuyer sur plusieurs boutons pour choisir entre la cuisson des frites, des légumes, du poulet ou d'un muffin. L'IA s'occupe de tout. La technologie Food Detect Pro regroupe 24 programmes automatiques pour un maximum de variété. Toutefois, il faut noter les limites de l'IA puisque parfois la technologie ne reconnaît pas ce qui se trouve dans le panier et il faut passer en mode manuel.
La détection peut aussi être gênée par une lumière trop vive, une lentille sale ou un panier chargé. Dans ce cas, le message "Unknown" s'affiche sur l'écran. Le Severin S-Fry Digital AI a un panier de 8 litres puisque ce modèle se destine aux grosses portions. Pour la puissance, c'est 1 800 W et une plage de température de 30 à 200 degrés.
L'airfryer est capable de frire à l'air chaud, de cuire au four, de rôtir et de garder les repas au chaud. Bien évidemment, si la proposition de l'IA ne convient pas, le réglage se modifie par soi-même. Pour le reste, il y a une fenêtre pour suivre la cuisson sans ouvrir le panier et des commandes via écran tactile en couleur.
En septembre dernier, le Severin S-Fry Digital AI a été présenté au salon IFA de Berlin. Severin cherche à présenter sa nouvelle vitrine technologique avec une stratégie claire : placer l'IA dans les appareils du quotidien.
Le Severin S-Fry Digital AI est le premier produit de cette nouvelle gamme axée sur l'IA. Parmi les autres appareils au programme, Severin lancera un aspirateur S-Power AI avec caméra pour repérer la saleté et adapter sa puissance. Sortie prévue en 2027.
Au programme, on trouve aussi un appareil de coiffure S-Style AI prévu pour le deuxième trimestre 2027, qui mesurera la distance avec le cuir chevelu pour ajuster la chaleur via IA. Le pari pour Severin, c'est de réduire le temps qu'on passe dans les menus si l'IA s'occupe de choisir le bon programme, la bonne température et la bonne durée.

articles.title: The Samsung S90H is an excellent OLED TV that delivers where it counts - and it's worthy rival to the LG C6
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Samsung S90H is an excellent mid-range OLED for watching movies and gaming, with a great viewing experience even in a bright room. While the picture requires some setup to get things just right and the sound could be better, it delivers a fantastic overall experience. It's a worthy rival to the LG C6, and for some, it may be their preferred choice of the two.
Reasons to buy
- + Exceptional picture quality
- + Effective OLED in bright rooms
- + Fantastic for gaming
Reasons to avoid
- - No Dolby Vision
- - Some black crush in darker scenes
- - Tizen has some annoyances
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Samsung S90H review: Two minute review
The Samsung S90H is the brand’s mid-range OLED TV for 2026. It delivers brilliant performance and features across the board, putting it up there with the best TVs of the year. While it doesn’t quite dethrone the rival LG C6 for me, the S90H proved to be a worthy opponent when I put the two side-by-side.
Picture quality is the S90H’s best highlight. With an effective anti-glare screen, it’s perfect for OLED viewing in a bright room, without many compromises. It delivers vibrant, punchy colors, powerful contrast and crisp, realistic textures. While there were black crush issues during some scenes, there were settings to mitigate this, meaning the S90H delivers picture quality that’s up there with the best OLED TVs.
The S90H is one of the best gaming TVs on the market. With a full suite of features, including 4K 165Hz and full VRR, and an ultra-low input lag time of 9.2ms (4K 60Hz), the S90H delivers strong gaming performance.
The S90H’s built-in sound is pretty good overall, being accurately connected to the action on screen, with punchy bass and good width. The S90H’s AI Sound is also competent and improves on the standard built-in sound, although I still found speech and mid-tones could get a bit muddled at times. While its built-in speakers are good enough for casual viewing, I’d recommend adding one of the best soundbars to match its fantastic picture.
Priced similarly to its rival LG C6, the S90H is very good value for money. It covers pretty much every base you’ll need and is available in sizes 42-83-inch. A 55-inch model will currently cost you $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,995, and while there are cheaper TVs with similar features available, the S90H offers great bang for your buck.
Samsung S90H review: Prices & release dates
- Release date: May 2026
- 42-inch: $999 / £899 / AU$1,995
- 48-inch: $1,099 / £999 / AU$2,395
- 55-inch: $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,995
- 65-inch: $1,499 / £1,6,99 / AU$3,995
- 77-inch: $2,499 / £2,499 / AU$5,495
- 83-inch: $3,499 / £3,599 / AU$7,495
As Samsung’s mid-range 2026 OLED TV, the S90H sits above the entry-level Samsung S85H and below the flagship Samsung S95H (known as the S99H in the UK). It’s available in six sizes, from 42-inch to 83-inch. The above prices are what you can expect to pay at the time of writing (November 2026).
The 55-inch model I tested launched for $1,999 / £1,799 / AU$2,995 in May/June 2026. Since its release, prices have fallen in all sizes in the US and UK, with the 55-inch model now priced at $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,995. (Prices remain unchanged in Australia.) The 55-inch LG C6, the S90H’s direct rival, currently retails for $999 / £1,199 / AU$2,495, and I expect the S90H’s prices will fall in line with the C6’s soon.

Samsung S90H review: Features
- Glare Free screen
- WOLED panel on 55-inch UK model
- NQ4 AI Gen 3 processor
Much like last year’s Samsung S90F, the panel on the S90H can vary based on size and region, though most models now seem to use a standard WOLED panel rather than a QD-OLED panel. Based on my measurements, I can confirm the 55-inch model I tested in the UK uses a WOLED panel.
The S90H has Samsung’s OLED Glare Free screen, which reduces mirror-like reflections in bright rooms. It uses Samsung’s NQ4 AI Gen 3 processor, the same one used in the flagship S95H/S99H, which has AI picture features such as Real Depth Enhancer Pro and AI 4K Upscaling Pro.
It supports HDR10+ enhanced HDR format, but like all Samsung TVs, there’s no support for Dolby Vision. For sound, the S90H supports Dolby Atmos but doesn't support DTS formats.
For audio, it uses a 2.1-channel, 40W speaker system and features Object Tracking Sound Lite (OTS Lite), a step-down version of the OTS+ used in the flagship S95H/S99H. There are two sound modes, Standard and Amplify, and a number of AI sound features, such as Adaptive Sound Pro and AI Sound Controller Pro.
The S90H supports 4K 165Hz, full VRR including AMD FreeSync and Nvidia G-Sync (the latter being introduced into Samsung’s TVs in 2025), ALLM, and HDR10+ gaming. These are featured in all four HDMI 2.1 ports.
Samsung’s own Tizen OS is the smart TV platform here. It features the Vision AI companion, which can be used to recommend content and help with settings. In terms of app support, the S90H supports all major streaming apps, including BBC iPlayer and ITVX for those in the UK.
- Features score: 5 / 5
Samsung S90H review: Picture quality
- Vibrant, punchy colors
- Effective glare screen
- Occasional black crush
Starting with brightness measurements, the S90H registered an impressive 1,689 nits peak HDR brightness (measured on a 10% window) in Filmmaker Mode, a great result for a mid-range WOLED TV that beats the LG C6’s 1,427 nits in the same tests. It also registered 305 nits fullscreen HDR brightness, again besting the C6’s 249 nits in the same tests.
When I compared the C6 and the S90H side by side, however, the C6 had higher perceived brightness, which I believe was the work of the C6’s processor. Still, in isolated viewing, the S90H’s picture looked bright, even in the often dim Filmmaker Mode. Movie Mode, which looks brighter in person, registered similar results in the same tests. Movie Mode does have Active Tone Mapping on by default (it’s set to Static in Filmmaker Mode), which would explain the added brightness in practice.
The S90H has Samsung’s OLED Glare Free screen, which is effective at reducing mirror-like reflections, meaning darker scenes are still visible in bright rooms. With Movie Mode on, I was even able to watch a challenging scene from The Batman with no reflections.
When watching daytime TV via Samsung TV Plus, the S90H’s upscaling proved effective. It sharpened textures for news broadcasts and streaming sports. Watching an HD movie, Treasure Planet on Disney Plus, the S90H again did a good job upscaling. Activating the Auto HDR Remastering feature boosted brightness, colors and contrast effectively. This feature also worked well for sports streamed through Prime Video, adding more depth to the picture.
Switching to reference 4K Blu-ray scenes, the S90H demonstrated excellent picture quality. It produced vibrant, punchy colors that looked great in scenes from Speed Racer, accurately rendering the vivid oranges, pinks, and yellows of the Racer family's candy-colored kitchen. In The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, Mario and Luigi’s red and green overalls were striking, and the Lumas had plenty of punch, which made the movie look fantastic.
Measuring HDR color gamut, the S90H hit 99.3% of the UHDA-P3 color space and 76.5% of the BT.2020 color space. These are great results in line with mid-range OLED rivals like the LG C6 and even flagship models like the Samsung S95H/S99H and LG G6 in the UHDA-P3 space, which is important for HDR content.
The S90H also demonstrated strong contrast, with a great balance between light and dark tones. Scenes from The Batman, whether it was the crime scene in Mayor Mitchell’s house or the Batcave, all looked fantastic, with bright lamps contrasting well with dark surroundings. The S90H’s blacks were inky and deep, and perfectly showcased in the shots of space from Project Hail Mary.
While the S90H does mostly deliver great shadow detail, with textures such as the roof and back wall of a dimly lit subway in The Batman still legible, this is where I noticed the S90H was prone to some black crush in its default Filmmaker Mode. Dark tones in movies like The Batman and Project Hail Mary looked too dark, resulting in occasional detail loss. Bumping up the Shadow Detail setting from 0 to the maximum 5 mitigated a lot of this, but there was still a hint of black crush in places.
Motion is very good on the S90H when you have the right settings. Watching a soccer game on Prime Video with the default settings, where Blur and Judder reduction are set to the maximum 10, resulted in some motion artifacts like ghosting of the ball. Reducing Blur to 3 and Judder to 5 or 6 resulted in smooth motion that didn’t look artificial. The same settings also worked well for movies, such as the high-speed races in Speed Racer and the Batmobile chase in The Batman.
Throughout viewing, textures looked very refined and realistic, giving everything a near-3D-like level of detail. People in particular looked incredibly lifelike, and with HDR pictures, everything looked crisp.
- Picture quality score: 5 / 5
Samsung S90H review: Sound quality
- 2.1 channel, 40W speakers
- Object Tracking Sound Lite (OTS Lite) is effective
- Mid-tones can be muddled
The S90H has a 2.1-channel, 40W speaker system and supports AI Sound features such as Adaptive Sound Pro and uses OTS Lite. There is support for Dolby Atmos, but not DTS. There are two sound modes to choose from: Standard and Amplify.
I was impressed by the S90H's punchy bass on its default Amplify settings, which did a good job rendering the rumble of the Batmobile’s engine in The Batman. During the same Batmobile chase scene, the S90H’s speakers delivered fantastic detail, such as swerving tyres and impacts with traffic, and the sound was accurately mapped to the action on screen, showing the effectiveness of the OTS system.
It also demonstrated a good balance between the score and other sound effects. While speech was mostly clear, it did get lost at times during the chaotic moments within the scene. I noticed too that mid-tones could get a bit muddled at times, but the sound was still very good.
Turning on the Adaptive Sound Pro setting in the AI Sound menu (found under the AI settings in the Advanced Features menu) yielded some good results, which I’ve not always found with AI sound modes on other TVs. More width was added, extending the sound further beyond the screen; the volume was louder overall, and more detail was produced. Bass was punchier, but it had lost the warmth of the default Amplify Mode. For a lot of viewing, you could get away with not using a soundbar, but the sound doesn’t quite match up to the picture’s excellence, so I’d recommend a soundbar for movies.
- Sound quality score: 4 / 5
Samsung S90H review: Design
- Razor-thin frame
- Lightweight but premium build
- SolarCell remote
The most striking thing about the S90H physically is its razor-thin frame. While there is a bit of bulk on the rear panel to accommodate speakers and various connections like HDMI ports, the top of the frame is incredibly slim. This gives it a sleek, modern appearance that makes the TV feel premium.
The S90H has a lightweight design, but still feels premium when viewed on its stand. The supplied plastic pedestal stand on my 55-inch review model did feel a little cheap compared to the rival LG C6's metal stand. However, once fully assembled, the TV was visually appealing.
As with most Samsung TVs, the S90H is supplied with Samsung’s SolarCell remote. While on the small side, the inclusion of Solar and USB-C rechargeable options is very useful. The design hasn’t changed much in the past few years, but honestly, it doesn’t need to.
- Design score: 4.5 / 5
Samsung S90H review: Smart TV & menus
- Tizen smart TV platform
- Easy-to-navigate menus
- Some odd quirks that can be annoying
Samsung’s own Tizen smart TV platform is used in the S90H and is generally a good, easy-to-use interface with useful hubs to divide up particular apps. The Home hub houses all apps and content recommendations, while the Game hub, naturally, houses everything to do with gaming.
Like many smart TV platforms, Tizen’s home screen features banner ads that take up about half the screen, pushing apps further down the page. I also found that, at times, Samsung TV Plus would autoplay the show I previously had on when I was trying to go to different sources. I found this frustrating, but eventually the S90H played ball.
There are a good number of picture settings on offer that can really make a difference (Shadow Detail being one of them), and they're fairly easy to find. Sound settings are a bit limited compared to other TVs I’ve tested. While the AI settings can help with this, they're kept in a separate menu. Overall, Tizen is a serviceable smart TV interface, but doesn’t quite match up to LG’s webOS or Roku.
- Smart TV & menus score: 4 / 5
Samsung S90H review: Gaming
- Four HDMI 2.1 ports
- Full suite of features
- Ultra-low 9.2 ms input lag
The S90H is well equipped for gaming, with four HDMI 2.1 ports that support 4K 165Hz, full VRR including AMD FreeSync and Nvidia G-Sync, ALLM, and HDR10+ gaming. It also has a Game hub where cloud gaming apps such as Xbox and Nvidia GeForce Now are housed, as well as links to Twitch streams.
The S90H's input lag measured an ultra-low 9.2ms at 4K 60Hz and 4.8ms at 1080p 120Hz. This performance translated when I was actually testing gaming on the S90H, with ultra-smooth motion during Battlefield V. As I whipped around missions, the S90H easily rendered all the action during high-intensity battles as I targeted enemies and dodged enemy fire.
The S90H’s excellent picture quality did wonders for games too, delivering crisp textures, balanced contrast and bold colors, all of which could be seen in various missions during Battlefield V.
- Gaming score: 5 / 5
Samsung S90H review: Value
- Similarly priced to rival OLEDs
- Great performance and features
- Cheaper mini-LED with similar features available
The S90H covers pretty much every base you’ll need, and while it would be nice to have Dolby Vision supported, the picture quality is good enough to do without it. The 55-inch model I tested has an MSRP of $1,999 / £1,799 / AU$2,995.
Since its release in May 2026, prices for the S90H have fallen, and at the time of writing (November 2026), a 55-inch model costs $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,995. While this puts it at the same price as the C6 in the UK, LG’s model is cheaper in the US and Australia at $999 / AU$2,495. I don’t expect the S90H to be more expensive for long, however, as prices will likely level out the further we get into its life cycle.
There are budget mini-LED TVs, such as the TCL QM7L/C7L, available for less that deliver great performance and features in their own right, but right now, the S90H is probably one of the best-value OLEDs you can get.
- Value score: 4.5 / 5
Should you buy the Samsung S90H?
| Samsung S90H |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | Full suite of features that covers nearly every base for movies and gaming | 5/5 | 
| Picture quality | Stunning colors, strong contrast and realistic textures. Also great for bright-room viewing thanks to its glare free screen | 5/5 | 
| Sound quality | Great detail and accuracy with punchy bass, but mid tones can sound muddled and sound could be wider | 4/5 | 
| Design | Premium build with sleek design, ultra-thin frame | 4.5/5 | 
| Smart TV and menus | Tizen is mostly good and easy to use, but has some quirks that can make it frustrating at times | 4/5 | 
| Gaming | Full suite of gaming features with ultra-smooth performance to match: a top-notch gaming TV | 5/5 | 
| Value | Fully specced mid-range OLED TV that might be pricier than rivals now, but prices will drop. | 4.5/5 | 
Buy it if...
You want superb OLED picture quality
The S90H's picture quality is excellent, delivering vibrant colors, powerful contrast, lifelike textures and great motion handling.
You want to watch OLED in a bright room
The S90H's glare-free screen is effective at eliminating reflections in bright rooms, meaning challenging dark scenes can even be watched in brighter conditions
You want an OLED for gaming
The S90H is fully equipped for gaming and delivers razor-sharp performance with smooth gameplay and brilliant picture quality
Don't buy it if...
You need Dolby Vision
Like all Samsung TVs, the S90H does not support Dolby Vision, which is used for streaming services, 4K Blu-ray and some gaming consoles. 
You don't want to set up your picture
The S90H delivers great picture quality, but you have to put in some work to get the picture just right, especially for darker scenes. 
You want the best smart TV platform
Tizen is mostly a good smart TV platform, but I found there were some frustrations from time to time.

| HDR support | HDR10+, HDR10, HLG | Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG | Dolby Vision, HDR10+. HDR10, HLG | HDR10+, HDR10, HLG | 
| Smart TV | Tizen | webOS 26 | Google TV | Samsung Vision AI (Tizen) | 
| HDMI ports | 4 x HDMI 2.1 | 4x HDMI 2.1 | 4 (2 x HDMI 2.1) | 4x HDMI 2.1 | 
LG C6
The S90H's biggest rival, the C6 is LG's mid-range 2026 OLED. It delivers similar excellent picture quality and features. The C6 is cheaper right now in some regions, but that could change soon. This one comes down to personal preference, although if you want an OLED for a bright room, the S90H is the better option. 
Read our full LG C6 review
TCL QM7L/C7L
The TCL QM7L (US)/C7L (UK/Aus) is the brand's mid-range SDQ mini-LED. While the S90H delivers better overall picture quality, the QM7L/C7L is better value for money, offering great picture quality and features for a fraction of the price. 
Read our TCL QM7L review and TCL C7L review
Samsung S95H/S99H
The Samsung S95H (US/Aus)/S99H (UK) is the flagship OLED in Samsung's lineup for 2026. It's brighter and has more refined picture quality than the S90H, but is significantly pricier. The S90H is better value for money in terms of price vs performance, but the S95H/S99H is the best choice if you want elite OLED. 
Read our Samsung S95H review and Samsung S99H review
How I tested the Samsung S90H
- Tested over a couple of weeks
- Tested using SDR and HDR sources in varying lighting conditions
- Measurements taken using Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software
I first tested the Samsung S90H over a few days with casual viewing to establish its best picture modes, landing on Filmmaker and Movie modes for movies and TV shows and Standard for sports and daytime TV.
I then commenced subjective testing. I watched reference scenes from 4K Blu-ray and other sources to test the S90H's picture quality, looking at color, contrast, detail, upscaling, textures, motion, and sound quality.
I then moved onto objective testing, taking measurements using specialized equipment. This included a Jeti Spectral 15VA spectroradiometer, profiled with a Klein K-10A colorimeter, a Murideo Six G 8K Metal test pattern generator, and Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software to record these measurements.
The first test I conducted was for brightness, measuring the S90H's HDR and SDR brightness using 1-100% sized white window test patterns, with the focus being on peak (10%) and fullscreen (100%) brightness.
Next, I tested the S90H's HDR color gamut coverage, focusing on UHDA-P3 (also known as DCI-P3) and BT.2020 color spaces.
I then tested the color and grayscale accuracy of the S90H in SDR, using the Delta-E averages (the margin of error between the test pattern source and what's shown on screen).
I also tested the S90H's HDR EOTF in 1,000, 4,000 and 10,000 nits. This test shows its accuracy at both light and dark levels. I also measured the S90H's Spectral Power Distribution, which demonstrates its color performance, using the Jeti spectroradiometer.
Finally, I tested the S90H's input lag using a Leo Bodnar 4K HDMI Input Lag Tester, measuring 4K 60Hz and 1080p 120Hz speeds in milliseconds.

articles.title: Criptomonedas: el precio de Bitcoin para este día
articles.text:
El bitcoin fue la primera criptomoneda que salió al mercado. Ideada por Satoshi Nakamoto en 2008, esta divisa digital promovía un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales luego de la crisis financiera mundial que se vivió ese año.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Valor de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
La cotización de bitcoin para este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) es de 75961.5 dólares, lo que significa que la criptomoneda sufrió un cambio de 0.21% en las últimas 24 horas.
Por otro lado, registró un cambio de 0.0% con respecto a su valor hace una hora. En cuanto a su popularidad, se ubica en la posición #1.
Bitcoin alcanza un nuevo récord y lidera el auge en el mercado de las criptomonedas
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.

articles.title: La RED Box Fibre combine petit prix et remboursement des frais de changement
articles.text:
Passer chez RED by SFR : une box à 22,99 € et jusqu’à 139 € récupérés
RED by SFR propose sa box fibre à 22,99 € par mois sans engagement. L’opérateur prévoit aussi jusqu’à 139 € de remboursements pour faciliter le changement.
Une box fibre à 22,99 € par mois, sans engagement
Changer de fournisseur Internet peut réserver quelques frais supplémentaires au moment de la souscription. RED by SFR tente de lever cet obstacle avec sa RED Box Fibre à 22,99 € par mois sans engagement. En plus de ce tarif accessible, l’opérateur propose de rembourser les 39 € de frais de mise en service et jusqu’à 100 € de frais de résiliation facturés par l’ancien fournisseur. Le coup de pouce peut donc atteindre 139 €, sur demande.
L’offre s’adresse aux foyers éligibles à la fibre qui souhaitent réduire leur facture sans s’engager sur une durée déterminée. Un point intéressant pour ceux qui hésitent encore à quitter leur opérateur actuel à cause des frais liés au changement.
La formule repose sur la Box 7 de SFR. Dans sa configuration de base, elle annonce un débit descendant et montant pouvant atteindre 1 Gb/s, avec le Wi-Fi 5. Une option à 1 € supplémentaire par mois permet de passer au Wi-Fi 6 et de profiter d’un débit descendant allant jusqu’à 2 Gb/s partagés, toujours avec 1 Gb/s en débit montant.
La téléphonie fixe est également incluse, avec les appels illimités vers les fixes de 100 pays. Les appels vers les mobiles en France peuvent être ajoutés pour 5 € par mois.
Côté télévision, l’application RED TV permet de retrouver des chaînes sur smartphone, tablette et ordinateur.
Jusqu’à 139 € remboursés pour faciliter le changement
L’argument financier ne se limite donc pas à l’abonnement mensuel. RED by SFR prévoit deux remboursements distincts, qui peuvent alléger la facture de départ :
-39 € de frais de mise en service remboursés sur demande, hors Box 5G.
-Jusqu’à 100 € de frais de résiliation de l’ancien opérateur pris en charge sur demande.
Le montant total peut ainsi atteindre 139 €. Il faut toutefois effectuer les démarches nécessaires pour bénéficier de ces remboursements : ils ne sont pas automatiquement déduits du prix affiché lors de la souscription.
La formule reste sans engagement, ce qui laisse la possibilité de changer à nouveau d’opérateur sans attendre la fin d'une période contractuelle. RED met également en avant son service client, avec 500 conseillers annoncés disponibles sept jours sur sept, de 8 h à 21 h.
Au final, la RED Box à 22,99 € par mois combine un tarif mensuel contenu et une aide financière appréciable au moment de changer de fournisseur. Les options peuvent faire grimper la facture, mais la formule de base devrait suffire aux foyers qui recherchent avant tout une connexion fibre et une offre sans engagement.

articles.title: Ethereum: cuál es la cotización de esta criptomoneda
articles.text:
Ether, comúnmente llamada como ethereum, es la moneda virtual #2 en cuanto a términos de capitalización de mercado, por lo que se trata de una de las divisas digitales que más despierta el interés entre los mineros (creadores de las criptodivisas).
Ethereum es una plataforma de blockchain de código abierto que se ejecuta con el uso de su moneda nativa, llamada ether o ETH, por lo que a pesar de que la gente usa estos nombres como sinónimos son cosas distintas.
Ether es un token que se utiliza específicamente en la blockchain ethereum para pagar transacciones. Este token es responsable de impulsar casi todo lo que ocurre en la red, misma que puede ser usada por cualquier persona para crear y ejecutar contratos inteligentes, que son programas de software que se ejecutan de manera autónoma y sin la intervención del usuario.
De acuerdo con el portal de Binance, la moneda digital solana actualmente cuenta con 122.2M de unidades creadas.
El costo de la criptomoneda ethereum para este día a las 14:05 horas (UTC) es de 2236.17 dólares. Esto quiere decir que la moneda digital registró un cambio de -0.18% en el último día, así como un movimiento de 0.0% en la última hora.
Por su nivel de capitalización, esta moneda digital ocupa la posición #2 entre las más populares.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Ethereum
Ethereum 2.0: las claves
Tras varios meses de retraso y con el temor de que ya nunca pasaría, finalmente el 15 de septiembre de 2022 Ethereum llevó a cabo su tan ansiada fusión o actualización al nuevo nivel 2.0 con la promesa de mejorar la experiencia de los usuarios de esta criptomoneda.
“The Merge”, inglés para “La Fusión”, es una transformación en la forma en que Ethereum procesa las transacciones y en cómo se crean nuevos tokens de Ether.
Esta fusión se trata de la combinación de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum con una nueva cadena de bloques separada conocido como proof-of-stake, el cual reduce el consumo de energía de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum en un 99,9 %, según sus propios desarrolladores, lo que la vuelve más “amigable” con el ambiente al tiempo que las transacciones serían más baratas.
Sus defensores creen que la fusión hará que Ethereum resulte favorecido con respecto al máximo rival, Bitcoin, pues podría aumentar su uso.
En el proceso Proof Stake los propietarios de Ether bloquearán cantidades establecidas de sus criptomonedas para verificar nuevos registros en la cadena de bloques, ganando nuevas monedas además de su criptografía “participada”.

articles.title: Ninja MultiPot XL : le multicuiseur qui veut en finir avec les cuissons en deux temps
articles.text:
Ninja MultiPot XL : le multicuiseur qui veut en finir avec les cuissons en deux temps
En plus de ses 11 modes de cuisson, le multicuiseur Ninja MultiPot XL se distingue par son système de cuves modulables. Celui-ci permet d'installer, au choix, un grand bac de 7 l ou deux récipients séparés de 3,1 l pour gérer simultanément deux préparations de repas différentes.
Le problème des multicuiseurs classiques ? Généralement, ils ne permettent de cuire qu'un seul plat à la fois. C'est pour répondre à cette problématique que Ninja a lancé, mercredi 28 octobre 2026, le MultiPot XL. Ce multicuiseur propose deux bacs de 3,1 l aux réglages indépendants. Une fonctionnalité qui permet de mener deux cuissons distinctes en même temps avec, à la clef, la promesse de gagner du temps au quotidien.
Chaque bac dispose de son propre couvercle en verre. Il est ainsi possible d'en ouvrir un, pour goûter ou pour assaisonner, sans interrompre la cuisson du second. Ces deux récipients peuvent également être retirés pour laisser place à une seule grande cuve de 7 l. Celle-ci, pensée pour régaler plus de 8 personnes, se traduit par un appareil au gabarit imposant : il faut compter 9 kg et 45 cm de profondeur. Des dimensions qui occuperont une place non négligeable sur le plan de travail.
11 programmes et des cuves adaptées à la cuisson au four
Dans le détail, le MultiPot XL développe 1 500 W sous le capot et propose 11 modes automatiques pour cuisiner : mijotage lent, vapeur, sous-vide, sauces, soupes, riz, pâtes, gâteaux ou encore confitures. Ninja intègre également un mode dédié pour saisir et rissoler les viandes. Bonne nouvelle pour la santé : les bacs du MultiPot XL, compatibles avec le lave-vaisselle, sont pourvus d'un revêtement en céramique antiadhésive garanti sans composés chimiques PFAS.
Si ce matériau évite les polluants controversés, il faudra aussi évaluer à l'usage si le multicuisueur de Ninja résiste bien aux rayures et si sa chauffe est homogène sur toute la surface. Les cuves ont également la particularité de supporter les fours traditionnels jusqu'à 220 °C, ce qui permet, par exemple, de gratiner un plat sans devoir le transvaser dans un autre ustensile.
Disponible à partir de 249,99 €, le Ninja MultiPot XL cible les foyers en quête d'un multicuiseur tout-en-un pour cuisiner des plats sans multiplier la vaisselle.

articles.title: "Debo una disculpa a mi familia": Jensen Huang confiesa su infidelidad mientras Nvidia investiga un posible espionaje chino
articles.text:
Una confesión personal y una investigación por posible espionaje chino han colocado a Jensen Huang en el centro de una noticia inesperada. El cofundador y CEO de Nvidia ha reconocido públicamente su infidelidad en un mensaje a sus empleados que comienza con una disculpa a su familia. Al mismo tiempo, el consejo de administración ha anunciado una investigación independiente para esclarecer las informaciones que señalan que Huang habría sido objetivo de una operación de inteligencia extranjera. Por ahora, la compañía sostiene que no tiene motivos para creer que se hayan visto comprometidos sus secretos empresariales o la seguridad nacional estadounidense.
El mensaje, que Nvidia ha hecho público, pone por escrito el alcance de su admisión: "Fui infiel a mi esposa. Mis actos le hicieron daño a ella y a nuestros hijos", escribió Huang. Añadió que asume la responsabilidad, acepta las críticas y espera reconstruir la confianza de su familia, aunque reconoce que una disculpa no puede deshacer lo sucedido. También pidió perdón a los trabajadores, al consejo de administración, a los socios y a los accionistas por no haber estado a la altura de su responsabilidad como CEO. Eso sí, en ningún momento identificó a la otra persona implicada.
La información disponible apunta a Alice Huang, una ciudadana china y exdirectiva de Megaspeed, una empresa de centros de datos con sede en Singapur que compra chips a Nvidia. Según The New York Times, los servicios de inteligencia estadounidenses consideran que la ejecutiva habría facilitado información a Pekín. El Financial Times informó posteriormente de un memorando de inteligencia que la vinculaba con el Ministerio de Seguridad del Estado chino y describía una supuesta relación sentimental entre ambos. Es importante señalar que el documento no se ha hecho público y las acusaciones no han sido demostradas. China, por su parte, ha rechazado las informaciones y las considera un intento de difamar al país.
Sospechas de espionaje chino
Para entender por qué este asunto ha despertado tanta atención en Washington, hay que mirar al negocio de los chips. Estados Unidos restringe la exportación a China de determinados procesadores avanzados utilizados para desarrollar sistemas de inteligencia artificial, aunque contempla licencias bajo ciertas condiciones. Megaspeed está bajo escrutinio estadounidense por sospechas de haber facilitado el acceso chino a tecnología restringida, algo que Huang rechazó al defender las operaciones comerciales con la empresa y asegurar que Nvidia había comprobado el destino de sus procesadores. Por otra parte, Singapur también mantiene abierta una investigación sobre la compañía, pero ha desmentido que sus autoridades investigaran a Alice Huang por sus presuntos vínculos con la inteligencia china.
Como decimos, con estas sospechas sobre la mesa, el consejo de administración del fabricante estadounidense ha decidido iniciar una investigación supervisada por consejeros independientes y asesores jurídicos externos. El procedimiento examinará la información disponible, con especial atención a la seguridad nacional y económica de Estados Unidos. El caso también ha llegado al Congreso, donde los presidentes de tres comisiones han solicitado una reunión informativa a puerta cerrada con Huang para el 18 de noviembre. Mientras tanto, el consejo mantiene su confianza en el ejecutivo, que se ha comprometido a colaborar plenamente, y un portavoz de la compañía ha confirmado que seguirá al frente de la compañía.

articles.title: El método con inteligencia artificial que utiliza una autoridad de Alemania para gestionar reclamos por privacidad
articles.text:
La autoridad de protección de datos de Hamburgo, en Alemania, usa un chatbot basado en un modelo de OpenAI para redactar borradores de cartas en la tramitación de quejas de privacidad. Lo detalló en un estudio de caso de nueve páginas del 5 de noviembre. El organismo recibió 4.220 reclamos en 2025, un 62% más que el año anterior.
El personal no creció al mismo ritmo, según el documento, y en 2026 las quejas siguen subiendo a una velocidad parecida. La autoridad, que responde al cargo de comisionado de Protección de Datos y Libertad de Información de Hamburgo, presenta el uso del chatbot como una herramienta de apoyo estrictamente limitada.
Las quejas pasaron de 2.607 en 2024 a 4.220 en 2025, según un comunicado de la propia autoridad del 8 de enero. El mayor salto se dio en redes sociales y sitios de citas: de 386 a 1.052. La mayoría apuntó a Facebook e Instagram, de Meta, por el uso de datos para entrenar su IA y por su modelo de pago o consentimiento.
Entre las causas del aumento, el comunicado menciona el uso creciente de herramientas de IA por parte de los ciudadanos, que facilitan informarse sobre sus derechos y presentar reclamos.
Un chatbot construido sobre el modelo GPT-5.6 Terra
El sistema se llama LLMoin. El gobierno de Hamburgo lo encargó pocos meses después del lanzamiento de ChatGPT y hoy está disponible para todas las autoridades de la ciudad y, cada vez más, para organismos de otros estados federales. Su núcleo es un modelo de OpenAI, actualmente GPT-5.6 Terra, alojado en la nube de Microsoft Azure.
El regulador parte de una premisa poco habitual: da por hecho que el modelo, con alta probabilidad, no es anónimo y puede contener datos personales absorbidos durante su entrenamiento. Se apoya en una opinión de diciembre de 2024 del comité que reúne a las autoridades de protección de datos de la Unión Europea, que permite usar esos modelos si el sistema impide que esos datos salgan.
Para eso, LLMoin aplica filtros de salida, un filtro que suprime contenido de odio, sexual, violento o de autolesión, instrucciones internas que prohíben tomar decisiones o revelar datos personales no aportados por el usuario, y pruebas de ataque simulado que encargó la Cancillería del Senado de Hamburgo. El regulador consideró suficientes esas medidas.
Las reglas: leer todo el expediente y revisar cada borrador
Según el estudio, los funcionarios deben leer primero el expediente completo y no guiarse por un resumen generado por IA. Después deciden qué tipo de carta enviar y qué argumentos incluir. El sistema solo ayuda a redactar y ordenar lo que los empleados ya resolvieron, y si faltan consideraciones, les pregunta por ellas. Los resultados deben revisarse siempre.
La autoridad prohíbe que el chatbot decida sobre las quejas o haga valoraciones jurídicas. Tampoco admite datos que requieran alta protección: las quejas sobre consultorios de psicoterapia o procesos penales, por ejemplo, las trata solo personal humano. El regulador no usa el sistema para redactar el aviso de derechos de apelación, porque debe reproducirse palabra por palabra.
El documento aclara que la ley no exige indicar en cada carta que fue redactada en parte con IA. La autoridad informa del uso en su política de privacidad. También reconoce que el sistema produce una estandarización notable del estilo con que el organismo se presenta al público.
Para 2027, la ciudad prepara una configuración con un modelo alojado en servidores propios de Dataport, el proveedor informático de la administración, con el objetivo de que el sistema pueda manejar datos de mayor confidencialidad.

articles.title: NVIDIA enquête sur la liaison de Jensen Huang avec une espionne chinoise présumée
articles.text:
NVIDIA ouvre une enquête indépendante pour déterminer si son patron a été ciblé par une opération de renseignement étrangère. Selon le New York Times, Jensen Huang a reconnu une relation intime avec Alice Huang, identifiée par les services américains comme travaillant pour Pékin.
L’affaire prend une nouvelle dimension pour NVIDIA. Après les révélations sur les liens entre Jensen Huang et Alice Huang, ancienne dirigeante d’un client du fabricant de puces, le conseil d’administration annonce une enquête ce dimanche 8 novembre. Le dirigeant, qui évoquait jusqu’ici des relations professionnelles ordinaires, a parallèlement adressé un message d’excuses aux salariés. Il conserve ses fonctions pendant les investigations.
Une enquête indépendante et une liaison désormais reconnue
Dans sa déclaration, le conseil annonce qu’un comité d’administrateurs indépendants supervisera les investigations, assisté d’avocats extérieurs indépendants. Il affirme n’avoir aucune raison de penser que la sécurité nationale américaine ou les secrets de NVIDIA ont été compromis, tout en s’engageant à examiner toutes les informations disponibles.
Selon le New York Times, Jensen Huang a reconnu devant le conseil avoir entretenu une relation intime avec Alice Huang, ancienne dirigeante de Megaspeed International, une entreprise singapourienne cliente de NVIDIA. Le quotidien affirme que les services américains ont conclu qu’elle travaillait pour le renseignement chinois, après avoir constaté qu’elle transmettait des informations à Pékin.
Dans un message aux salariés reproduit par Bloomberg, le dirigeant reconnaît son infidélité : « J’ai été infidèle à mon épouse ». Il présente ses excuses à sa famille et aux équipes, puis assure, concernant les investigations : « Je soutiens cette enquête et coopérerai pleinement …
Son mémo ne nomme toutefois pas Alice Huang. Et les informations rapportées sur ses activités présumées ne permettent pas d’établir que Jensen Huang lui aurait transmis des secrets de NVIDIA. C’est notamment ce risque que l’enquête doit permettre d’éclaircir.
Les relations avec Megaspeed déjà sous surveillance à Washington
L’affaire avait déjà atteint le Congrès. Trois présidents de commissions de la Chambre des représentants demandent à entendre Jensen Huang à huis clos le 18 novembre, sur ses interactions avec Alice Huang et les protections de l’entreprise contre l’espionnage étranger.
Les enjeux dépassent la vie privée du dirigeant. NVIDIA fournit des composants essentiels aux infrastructures d’intelligence artificielle, dont les exportations vers la Chine font l’objet de restrictions américaines. Son patron est également un interlocuteur influent de Donald Trump sur ces questions.
Megaspeed est, de son côté, visée par une enquête du département américain du Commerce sur un possible contournement de ces restrictions, selon le New York Times. Ce dossier reste distinct de la question d’une éventuelle fuite de renseignements par l’intermédiaire du dirigeant. Pékin a précédemment rejeté les accusations d’espionnage.
NVIDIA n’a pas annoncé de date pour les conclusions des investigations. Le conseil promet de communiquer de nouveaux éléments lorsque cela sera approprié, tandis que Jensen Huang s’engage à coopérer pleinement.

articles.title: AI cyber resilience and the trust gap - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI cyber resilience and the trust gap
Backup and recovery has evolved into data protection, security and cyber recovery. Today, the focus is on business resilience. The scope continues to expand, with growing attention to how attackers use artificial intelligence and how defenders can use it to better protect their assets.
In new field research with our partner Qualitate, we explored these issues, including a less frequently discussed risk: What happens when AI deployed inside an enterprise makes a mistake?
Our research indicates that confidence in recovery is running well ahead of capabilities. The study underscores the immaturity of cyber resilience and AI security. Agentic AI is putting more pressure on practitioners to secure their data, reconstruct an agent’s actions, understand what it was trying to accomplish and confidently restore the business to a trusted state. The risks created by an enterprise’s own AI deployments are becoming a growing part of the resilience challenge.
Welcome to Breaking Analysis No. 333, AI cyber resilience and the trust gap. In this episode, we welcome back Krista Case, who recently conducted in-depth interviews with 25 security and cyber resilience practitioners as part of theCUBE Research’s Cybersecurity & Resilience Summit.
Access the full slide deck and appendix with survey details and practitioner quotes.
Study objectives and scope
Information technology and security practitioners face two growing pressures: 1) Protecting the business from adversaries using AI and 2) Putting guardrails in place as their own organizations move AI projects into production. Our study examined how organizations are approaching security and resilience across both fronts, with particular attention paid to the risks created by their own AI deployments.
We explored how organizations are managing agent identity, permissions, monitoring, etc., alongside their preparations for incident response and recovery. A central question was what happens when an agent takes an incorrect action using legitimate permissions. That scenario raises three questions:
- Reconstruction: Can the organization establish what the agent did?
- Downstream effects: Can it determine the consequences for affected systems and business processes?
- Recovery: Can it recover those business processes?
These questions shaped our study into how organizations are preparing for AI to take a more active role in their operations. As agents gain the authority to act, practitioners need to understand how a mistake could spread and what recovery would require.
Ultimately, the study examined organizations’ readiness to secure their own AI deployments and recover from mistakes made by authorized agents, alongside the continuing need to defend against adversarial AI.
Confidence is running ahead of tested recovery
Our study identified just four of 25 organizations as having exercised an AI or agent incident scenario, including partial exercises. We believe this finding exposes a core trust gap at the center of the research: Confidence in recovery often runs ahead of what organizations have actually tested.
These findings come from a small sample of in-depth interviews conducted with our partner Qualitate. The conversations allowed us to explore what customers have tested, the additional security work their own AI creates and what it takes to resume a business process safely. One healthcare practitioner phrased the disconnect between confidence and readiness as follows:
No, we have not completed any tabletop exercises as it pertains to an AI agent or other similar attacks. We’re highly confident because these are scenarios similar to non-AI incidents we have handled before.
— Senior manager, information security operations, healthcare and biotech
Across the interviews, respondents who did express confidence often drew heavily on existing ransomware and incident response playbooks. Their experience with non-AI incidents understandably provides a degree of trust. But it also raises a concern in that organizations may assume that an agent taking an incorrect action can be handled in the same way as an insider or external attacker doing something similar. We don’t believe existing playbooks cover all scenarios.
Rather, we believe that assumption needs to be tested against the specific demands of an agent incident. The interviews revealed a mixed picture of true validation:
- Partial exercises: The four identified cases include limited exercises, so the count itself is not a signal for mature trust and should not be read as four demonstrations of complete business recovery;
- Individual controls: Other respondents described testing permissions, containment and the like. Those tests provide useful evidence about particular controls while broader recovery questions remain.
Complete business recovery requires an organization to reconstruct a sequence of authorized actions, identify incorrect outcomes, repair downstream effects and safely resume the affected business process. Demonstrating that the full sequence works is a nontrivial exercise.
The speed, scale and interconnected nature of agent activity makes that even more challenging. Actions can affect multiple systems and processes, creating consequences that existing playbooks need to account for. We see a risk of false confidence when organizations assume that their experience with traditional non-AI incidents will translate automatically. Testing needs to establish how well their capabilities hold up under the conditions an agent can create, which may be novel.
Bottom line: Evidence of validated, end-to-end business recovery from an agent incident remains limited in our study. We believe organizations should exercise their existing playbooks against realistic agent scenarios, with safe business resumption as the measure of success.
Validating tools across the full agent workflow
Our interviews raised questions about tooling, maturity and the processes needed to prove that existing capabilities work for agentic AI. Two findings as shown below highlight the limited reach of detection and reconstruction capabilities in the organizations studied:
- Only two of 25 respondents reported broad detection of anomalous or unintended agent behavior;
- Only three of 25 respondents reported broad monitoring and reconstruction of agent activity.
One healthcare practitioner’s assessment of the controls already implemented underscores the trust gap:
No, for the ones that have been implemented, we have not tested or validated that they work.
— Senior manager, information security operations, healthcare and biotech
Enterprises already have identity systems, application logs, data protection tools and the like, along with established incident response processes. They are trying to extend these capabilities to AI. The central challenge is validating that the tools can reconstruct activity across an entire agent workflow.
Agents interact with multiple applications, invoke tools and autonomously trigger downstream actions. Each system may capture its own events without providing a coherent record of the complete workflow. Incident response requires correlating those records to establish which agent acted and under what authority, then tracing the tools it invoked and the changes that resulted.
This reminds us of the early days of disaster recovery, when organizations would test failover but hesitate to test failback because they were nervous about what might happen. We see a similar reluctance to ask questions that could expose gaps in readiness or cause downstream problems. The concern is whether the connected tools and processes will hold up under realistic agent incident conditions.
Bottom line: Organizations need to exercise the full agent workflow under realistic conditions, including a plausible worst-case event, and validate that their tools and processes can reconstruct the activity and support the response.
Restoring a trusted business service
Our assessment of the field interviews highlights both the technical and business dimensions involved in a recovery. An AI agent can use legitimate access to change a record incorrectly or send a message that should never have been sent. A backup may work and the restored systems may appear healthy while the business remains unable to resume safely.
StorageTek veteran Fred Moore, an early mentor to Dave Vellante, coined the phrase: “Backup is one thing, recovery is everything.” The scope of recovery continues to expand as organizations consider the consequences of agents acting across business systems.
A director of information security at a media and entertainment firm described the problem this way:
We could restore our systems, we could restore within our recovery objectives, but that doesn’t necessarily guarantee that it’s safe. The bottleneck here would be trust.
— Director of information security, media and entertainment
Recovery point objectives or RPO and recovery time objectives or RTO are the so-called business metrics. But business users need more meaningful key performance indicators that resonate — specifically, what a trusted, viable service looks like and how that condition can be verified. That includes establishing who needs to participate in recovery and who signs off that operations can safely resume.
This direction needs to come from the top down; and be verified bottom up. Business leaders must define the requirements, with IT and security acting as partners to provide the underlying technology and help achieve the required outcome. The responsibility extends beyond the traditional data protection team’s work of recovering data and systems.
Incorrect transactions, human error and failures that ripple across systems have existed for a long time. Agentic AI adds two complications:
- Speed and scale: Incorrect actions can propagate rapidly across the environment, increasing the scope of the incident;
- Tracing the activity: Teams need to understand the agent’s access and intended task, establish what actions it took and follow the downstream effects.
That requires a comprehensive view of what went wrong and what needs to happen to recover. The organization must be able to trace the agent’s activity and evaluate the resulting business state against clear criteria for safe operation.
Bottom line: Recovery requires explicit criteria for verifying that a business service can be trusted and clear responsibility for approving its return to operation. The business must set that direction, with IT and security providing the capabilities to carry it out.
Human oversight can mask a recovery gap
Humans in the loop help organizations restrict what agents can do. Resilience also has to account for what happens when a human misses an incorrect action or cannot keep pace with agents operating at machine speed. Two statements from the same CIO illustrates the issue:
So the given scenario will be detected by human beings before the AI agents can take the actions.
If it really happens, currently we do not have the capability to roll back the agent’s action.
— Chief information officer, real estate and construction
The first statement shows confidence that human oversight will catch the problem. The second acknowledges a missing “undo command” if the human oversight fails. This captures why approvals and recovery testing need to advance together. Reliance on human intervention can bring a false sense of security and defer attention to the recovery details needed when a mistake gets through.
Our field study also revealed how customers are weighing the tradeoffs around autonomy, with organizations generally still containing what their agents can do. Those decisions become particularly important when agents receive authority to take remedial actions during an incident or recovery.
The level of autonomy granted should reflect the risk of the action. Before allowing an agent to approve or execute a remedial action, organizations need to understand the consequences of an incorrect decision. That calls for a tiered approach built around two considerations:
- Action risk: What could happen if the agent makes a mistake, and what level of risk is the organization willing to tolerate?
- Guardrails: What authority should the agent have, and what limits need to surround its ability to act?
We expect human approval to become an increasingly significant bottleneck over the next six to 12 months. Organizations need to establish these boundaries as they begin trusting agents to take more remedial actions.
Bottom line: Human oversight and recovery testing need to develop together. As organizations delegate more authority to agents, they must account for mistakes, the limits of human review and the risk associated with each action.
Rehearsing agent recovery in a replica environment
A retail practitioner described a viable approach to rehearsing an agent incident and we see this as a best practice. Specifically, this firm replays the agent’s actions in a replica environment, investigating the root cause and using granular snapshots to understand the transactional effects. The respondent explicitly confirmed that the approach had been tested in the sandbox with the following statement:
Yes, if the agent went across multiple systems, my approach is to replay this within my sandbox environment, which is a full replica of all of the systems.
— Director of information technology, retail
The value of this approach is in reproducing the sequence of events and investigating their effects across systems. Our assessment of what such an exercise should confirm is anchored on three outcomes:
- A trace of the incident: Reconstruct what happened across the affected systems;
- A defined scope for remediation: Identify the root cause and affected transactions;
- A path back to a trusted business state: Establish how the consequences can be addressed and recovery can proceed.
We see these as minimum viable expectations for the evidence an exercise should produce.
We use the term digital twin here as a broad analogy for this approach. A fuller digital twin would involve a richer representation of business processes, dependencies and state. We believe the industry still has work to do in that direction, and that work will become more important as enterprises use AI to run critical functions. In addition, it will further expand the notion of recovery as the state of the business will become increasingly more complicated as agents perform more of the work.
The respondent also acknowledged a limitation saying: larger transaction volumes could require more time for reconciliation. Replaying actions and identifying affected transactions provides useful information, while the time needed to resolve their consequences remains an open item. Richer simulations of business environments could help organizations test agent behavior and prepare for what a failure might look like in production.
In other words, testing the recovery sequence in a variety of scenarios inside a digital twin of the business prior to pushing the process into production. Further, this “red teaming” exercise must be ongoing – expanding the concept of continuous data protection into the state of a firm’s operations in more granular snapshots.
Bottom line: This example offers a practical approach to reproducing agent actions, investigating their consequences and rehearsing recovery. Its value also points toward the need for richer representations of the business processes those agents affect.
More autonomy requires demonstrated recovery
If a chief information security officer takes one action from this study, we recommend exercising an agent incident affecting one consequential workflow already in production. Choose a workflow in which an agent has permission to act across multiple systems, and design the exercise to include incorrect actions taken with valid credentials and permissions.
The exercise should also include a scenario requiring human approval. This helps establish the boundaries around where autonomy is appropriate and where human oversight remains necessary.
The practical steps are as follows:
- Establish what the agent can reach: Identify the systems it can access and the actions it is authorized to take;
- Demonstrate containment: Test whether the agent can be stopped, its access revoked and further tool use prevented. These “kill switch” capabilities are important to limiting the scope of an incident;
  - Ensure the conditions that flip a kill switch are determined and controlled by you, the customer;
- Reconstruct and correct: Establish what the agent did, whether the consequences can be repaired and what unresolved exceptions or residual effects remain;
- Demonstrate safe resumption: Produce evidence that the affected business process is ready to resume and establish who approves that decision;
Validation by the business owner is essential. Security teams can establish that an incident has been contained and provide evidence of what happened. The business owner must determine whether the resulting business state is acceptable. That decision needs to account for the consequences of the agent’s actions and any remediation work still required.
The exercise should document what was proved, what remains untested and which teams are responsible for closing the remaining gaps. That evidence should also inform decisions about how much authority an agent receives. The organization needs to understand its ability to reverse or correct actions and recover their consequences as it considers granting greater autonomy.
Build resilience into agent deployments from the start
The discussions at the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit reinforced the themes emerging from the field study. Conversations with vendors, practitioners and researchers underscored the need to build resilience and recovery into agent deployments from the outset. Evidence that these capabilities work becomes essential as agentic workloads move into production.
The challenge includes preserving and recovering a trusted business state when an agent produces an incorrect outcome despite having legitimate credentials. Organizations need to understand how those outcomes affect their operations and what it will take to address them.
Existing investments in data protection infrastructure, security and recovery remain critical. The work ahead is to identify the gaps that emerge under the new requirements and pressures created by enterprise AI. That requires collaboration across internal teams and with vendors to understand where capabilities need to improve.
Bottom line: We believe trust in enterprise AI requires tested evidence that organizations can understand what agents have done, stop them, reconstruct their actions and recover to a healthy business state. Our research indicates that organizations still have work to do to demonstrate that their existing security and recovery capabilities can meet that requirement.

Lisser, onduler ou boucler

Les Kiss' Wallabies tenure has already had its fair share of euphoric highs and crushing lows

Les Kiss has since replaced Joe Schmidt at the Wallabies helm, and it's been a topsy-turvy start for the former rugby league player. After winning a double-header against Japan and even toppling South Africa, they were held by Argentina before a Bledisloe Cup annihilation at the hands of New Zealand.
Kiss is very much in the experimental phase of his tenure, but even so his decision to call up 37-year-old Kurtley Beale, five years after his last cap, has raised eyebrows. At the other end of the spectrum, Teddy Wilson, the uncapped son of former Wallabies captain David, has also been brought into the setup.

On the contrary, Borthwick was rewarded with a contract extension in September, and it's since emerged that he recently turned down the services of the legendary Shaun Edwards, the best defensive coach in the game.
