articles.title: There’s no slowing down media’s pivot-to-video 2.0
articles.text:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the pressures of creating content for the internet, follow Mia Sato. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
There’s no slowing down media’s pivot-to-video 2.0
Just as publishers are starting to crack the vertical video code, social media platforms are looking ahead to a new format.
There’s no slowing down media’s pivot-to-video 2.0
Just as publishers are starting to crack the vertical video code, social media platforms are looking ahead to a new format.
How it started
Almost exactly a decade ago, the media industry was in the middle of a video revolution — or so it thought. In the mid-2010s, publications poured money into burgeoning social media video efforts, chasing the promise of reaching larger audiences and opening new lines of revenue. Print publications and digital news outlets alike hired teams, pumped out content, and entrusted platforms like Facebook with their reach and distribution.
That pivot-to-video slowly revealed itself to be a lot of smoke and mirrors when it became clear that Facebook had inflated video views. Newsrooms cut writers and editors in a move to video — and then cut those video teams when they realized the pivot had not paid off. For many in the media industry, social video brings to mind layoffs and instability rather than the promised abundance.
A “pivot” feels inadequate to describe the current emphasis on social video, not just in newsrooms but in society writ large. Social media companies have reorganized their feeds to emphasize video, spurred by the massive growth of TikTok during the pandemic. But the media industry is still playing catch-up, and in some cases it seems to have been slow to jump in (perhaps cautious given past experience). It took years for some publishers to start incorporating vertical video on their websites, apps, and stories, for example, and it takes coordination and intention to get individual reporters in front of a camera to talk about their work. In the meantime, YouTube has become the most popular streamer, commanding nearly 16 percent of TV viewing, according to Nielsen. Twenty percent of Americans regularly get news from TikTok, and that number jumps to 39 percent for people 18 to 29 years old, Pew found.
Viewers favor the stripped-down selfie-style video dispatches from personalities they trust, even if those creators are not themselves reporting and writing the news. Compared with a decade ago, the barrier to entry and cost of making video content has plummeted: Anyone with a smartphone can become a video creator, no fancy equipment or editing needed. Social video is fast, personality-driven, casual, and, at times, unfiltered — the exact opposite from what news outlets are used to. A second pivot-to-video is underway, and the media industry once again wants in.
How it’s going
Video is unavoidable on social media, if not an expected part of how people and institutions show up online. TikTok’s influence is felt everywhere: on competitor platforms like Meta’s Reels and YouTube Shorts, of course, but also in unexpected places, like LinkedIn. There are no signs of it slowing down, either: The time spent watching Reels on Facebook was at an all-time high in Q3. Early tests in other countries suggest Meta is toying with the idea of dropping users directly into full-screen video upon opening the Instagram and Facebook apps. The appetite for video seems insatiable, and if news organizations won’t lean in, armies of content creators will be happy to scoop up the audiences.
Some news outlets were relatively early to the short-form social video boom. The Washington Post, for example, found notable success on TikTok before many peers had even created dedicated accounts on the platform. (Dave Jorgenson, the face of the Post’s social video effort, left the paper last year. He now makes short and longform videos under Local News International — perhaps a testament to the trust that viewers place in individual creators.)
Beyond having a short-form video presence, some traditional news outlets are leaning into formats and styles popularized in the vertical video era. CNN partnered with Jubilee, the popular channel that produces debate-me-style videos on hot-button political topics. The CNN town hall with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico was conducted in the Jubilee style. The New York Times, which for years has produced polished documentary-style videos, recently introduced the vertical video series “The Call.” Unlike the Times’ more buttoned-up videos, the point of “The Call” is to create a sense of intimacy, like you’re getting updates from a friend: The show’s host ostensibly makes a video call to a journalist reporting on the ground to ask them about what they’re witnessing.
News outlets are also directly hiring or working with content creators. Some outlets like The Washington Post have spun up so-called creator networks, where they partner with influencers to produce content independent from the newsroom. A new program supported by Poynter and Microsoft pairs content creators with a handful of news outlets so they can create content tailored for social media.
And then, of course, there are the clips. Podcasts became videos, which became bite-sized clips of podcasts formatted for vertical feeds. TV shows became web shows, which gave rise to microdramas. News articles — even major investigations — are now adapted for vertical video audiences. Individual reporters (myself included) make talking-head clips explaining our reporting. Earlier this year, I called this phenomenon “the clippening”: the reformatting of all media to be legible in a vertical video feed, even if the original work is neither vertical nor video. It’s hard to fault the people and institutions putting resources into social video — audiences are consuming it — but it’s also feeling a lot like the past.
One of the misguided beliefs of pivot-to-video 1.0 was that traction, views, or engagement on social media platforms would be enough to offset (and ideally surpass) the cost of making the content. For many, that ended up not being true, with flawed metrics, of course, being part of the reason: Virality feels nice, but monetizing that attention isn’t always straightforward. These days, social media companies have largely coalesced around the “views” measurement meaning the number of times a post was served up on somebody’s feed, whether they watched the whole thing or swiped away immediately. How many people who watch a clip of a podcast go on to listen to the full episode? Are the people watching my TikToks about my stories actually going to The Verge to read it, or buying a subscription to support my work? You can’t eat views.
The hope is that we will find new audiences where they’re already spending time. There are millions of people discussing news that journalists are uncovering — it’s important that we reach them, build trust, and be part of the conversation. What’s certain is that if reporters and news outlets don’t, a whole slew of creators will be there to take their place.
What happens next
Just as we’re getting used to short form, the ground is once again shifting under our feet. Not content simply being social media, platforms are looking to be a destination for longer form, higher production quality entertainment. Tech companies know that people watch videos on their phones, but they would also really like users to watch on their televisions, too.
This spring, YouTube’s pitch to content creators (and advertisers) was to make exclusive shows for the platform. YouTube is dominating the TV streaming wars, but other platforms like Instagram are pushing in that direction, too: Its recently announced “Features” effort allows for 90-minute horizontal video uploads, and it seems to be specifically angling for television viewing. (Unsurprisingly, there are a lot of questions from creators about what they get in return for posting longer content.) Some news outlets are already thinking ahead and eyeing longform. The BBC struck a deal with YouTube in early 2026 to create special programming specifically for the platform, then followed it up by announcing a 24/7 YouTube livestream in an effort to reach young people.
Short form isn’t going anywhere, at least right now. But these efforts to move into longer, more resource-intensive video content could be a harbinger of what’s to come — and what could soon be asked of news publishers and influencers alike. News media have had a complicated relationship with tech platforms. On one hand, it’s where audiences are, and platforms allow publishers to reach those people. On the other hand, tech companies signal to outlets (and creators) what kind of content they should prioritize, and everyone has to scramble to meet the new demand. Just as soon as journalists start getting comfortable with front-facing selfie videos, we may be facing a whole new beast: videos that are horizontal and longer, with a higher production value and higher barrier to entry that we typically associate with TV and streaming.
By the way
- Instagram is already starting to place horizontal videos in discovery feeds — I recently saw the format bumped to the top of my Explore tab, mixed in with photos and vertical Reels.
- Even platforms like X that are traditionally associated with text-based content are trying to sweeten the deal to get users to post more videos. The company has an invite-only bonus program that pays creators who post videos regularly. Screenshots shared by X staff indicate that creators can make thousands of dollars for posting vertical videos under 3 minutes.
- If you feel like you’ve been seeing a lot more New York Times Cooking videos, it’s not your imagination: It’s a deliberate strategy to make video content from non-news verticals at the company.
Read (or watch) this
- It would only be appropriate to include a video here, given the topic this week. Here’s Instagram head Adam Mosseri trying to explain the about-face the platform is doing around longform video. The comments on YouTube hammer home a big question: Instagram benefits from more content like this, but what’s in it for creators (and, by extension, news outlets)?
- Short-form audiences were recently described as “rented attention” in the Link In Bio newsletter. Could longer-form content create more durable, lasting relationships between creator (or news org) and audience? Longer formats could put pressure on creators to deliver higher-quality, more in-depth material that is harder to fake than in a quick-hit 60-second clip.
- News publishers are in a constant push and pull with the platforms that make their work discoverable — and not just with social media. Consider Google’s AMP page format, for example, which promised to make the mobile web a better experience for readers. This quote, from my colleague David Pierce’s 2023 story about AMP, really sums up the relationship:
  - “If Google said, ‘you must have your homepage colored bright pink on Tuesdays to be the result in Google,’ everybody would do it, because that’s what they need to do to survive,” says Terence Eden, a web standards expert and a former member of the Google AMP Advisory Committee.

articles.title: Canva entlässt Hunderte Mitarbeiter – und wird von der Online-Community dafür gefeiert
articles.text:
Massenentlassungen bei Canva: Warum das Unternehmen trotzdem gefeiert wird
Laut Layoffs.fyi haben allein in diesem Jahr weltweit 350 Startups und Tech- Firmen Stellen gestrichen. Mehr als 142.000 Beschäftigte sind betroffen. Dass auch Canva Personal entlässt, ist daher kaum überraschend. Bemerkenswert ist allerdings, wie das Unternehmen mit diesem Schritt umgeht – und dass die Online-Community es genau dafür feiert.
22 Prozent von Änderungen betroffen
„Heute habe ich ein paar zutiefst schwierige Neuigkeiten mitzuteilen“, leitete Canva-Gründerin und CEO Melanie Perkins ihre E-Mail an die Mitarbeiter:innen ein, die sie auch auf Linkedin teilte. „Wir haben die sehr harte Entscheidung getroffen, einschlägige Änderungen in unserer Organisationsstruktur vorzunehmen.“ Insgesamt 1.271 Menschen verlieren ihre Stelle oder wechseln auf andere Positionen. Somit sind 22 Prozent der gesamten Belegschaft betroffen.
Laut Unternehmen stelle das einen wichtigen Schritt dar, um sich auf das nächste Kapitel vorzubereiten – womit der für 2027 geplante Börsengang gemeint sein könnte. Wie unter anderem Golem berichtet, sind die Kosten durch die Einführung diverser KI-Tools drastisch gestiegen. Wachstum und Umsatz blieben zuletzt hinter den Erwartungen zurück. Die Bewertung von Canva sank demzufolge von 42 auf 34,9 Milliarden Dollar. Für den Börsengang muss das Unternehmen jetzt also offenbar sparen.
Canva-CEO findet einfühlsame Worte
Im Rahmen der Umstrukturierung will Canva Produkt-, Wachstums- und Plattform-Teams zu einer Produktorganisation zusammenfassen, Hierarchien abbauen und die Eigenverantwortung stärken. Sydney soll zum Hauptstandort für einen größeren Teil der verbleibenden Mitarbeiter:innen werden, was für einige Umzüge nach sich ziehen wird. Ab Januar sollen die meisten, die im Hybridmodell arbeiten, zudem an zwei bis drei Tagen pro Woche ins Büro kommen.
Angesichts der drastischen Änderungen findet Perkins mitfühlende Worte für diejenigen, die bleiben und teils drastische Einschnitte erleben werden, sowie für diejenigen, die das Unternehmen verlassen müssen. „Dies ist zweifellos der schwerste Moment in unserer dreizehnjährigen Geschichte. Hinter jeder Entscheidung steht jemand, der uns sehr am Herzen liegt, und ich weiß, dass die Folgen für die direkt Betroffenen, ihre Familien, Freund:innen und Teamkolleg:innen sehr real sein werden.“
Auf Social Media wird Canva gefeiert
Wer seinen Job verliert, geht allerdings nicht leer aus. Unabhängig vom Standort werden Gehälter mindestens sechs Monate lang weiter gezahlt. Wer erst im vergangenen Jahr bei Canva angefangen hat, muss für Aktienoptionen keine Sperrfrist abwarten. Krankenversicherungen sollen zwölf Monate lang bestehen bleiben. Auch ihren Firmen-Laptop dürfen entlassene Mitarbeiter:innen behalten. Dazu kommen Coachings und Förderungen für Personen, die selbst gründen möchten.
Die Reaktionen auf dieses Abfindungspaket fallen äußerst positiv aus. „Eine wirklich beeindruckende, einfühlsame, transparente und großzügige Art, eine zweifellos sehr schwere Entscheidung zu kommunizieren“, schrieb ein:e Nutzerin laut Fast Company auf Linkedin. Eine weitere Person fügte hinzu: „Viele Unternehmen werden in diesem Jahr Entlassungen vornehmen. Nur wenige werden dies so handhaben wie hier.“ Auf Instagram wird sogar scherzhaft gefragt, wo man sich bewerben muss, um von Canva entlassen zu werden.
Der entscheidende Unterschied?
Auch in der deutschsprachigen Linkedin-Community sind die Reaktionen weitestgehend positiv. „Ich glaube, jedes Unternehmen braucht auch eine Frau als CEO. Und Canva liefert mir gerade wieder einen Grund dafür“, schreibt beispielsweise Alena Brügger in einem Post. Wegen seiner weiblichen Führung stach Canva schon seit Langem aus der ansonsten männlich dominierten Tech-Branche heraus. Fortune beschrieb Canva kürzlich sogar als das „weltweit am höchsten bewertete Startup, das von einer Frau gegründet wurde und von einer Frau geführt wird“. Ob dieser Faktor tatsächlich etwas mit der Art und Weise zu tun hat, wie das Unternehmen mit den Entlassungen umgeht, bleibt offen.

articles.title: De la nevera al agua del grifo o la luz: los ciberataques ya impactan en la vida cotidiana
articles.text:
De la nevera al agua del grifo o la luz: los ciberataques ya impactan en la vida cotidiana
La inteligencia artificial dispara la frecuencia, rapidez y efectividad de los incidentes digitales, que cada vez suponen un riesgo mayor para las infraestructuras críticas
Subir la temperatura de neveras en supermercados de 12 países para estropear toneladas de comida. Dejar colgadas las webs de medio mundo. Ejecutar el mayor robo de la historia. Acceder a datos personales del primer ministro surcoreano y su gabinete. Y al historial médico e información financiera de casi medio millón de moldavos. Este es el resumen de lo que han conseguido los ciberataques más relevantes solo en las últimas dos semanas. Si ampliamos el foco hasta el verano podemos sumar a la lista problemas en la distribución de agua en 12 Estados de EE UU o el hackeo del sistema de salud australiano. Los analistas temen que esta sea la nueva normalidad: un escenario en el que todo, también el mundo físico, se puede tambalear a golpe de teclado y movimiento de ratón.
Vivimos un cambio de era. Los ciberataques se han disparado en los últimos tiempos, tanto en cantidad como en calidad. El número de incidentes registrados aumenta año tras año con cifras de dos dígitos (en España, un 24%, según datos del Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad). Y, tal y como demuestra el episodio de las neveras, el poder de los hackers va más allá de sustraer datos o extorsionar a empresas: también son capaces de intervenir en el funcionamiento de infraestructuras críticas.
Can we please stop posting about rogue AI and how it’ll kill us and go back to posting about all the cool vulns it is finding?
— Charlie Miller (@0xcharlie) September 12, 2026
La inteligencia artificial (IA) es la responsable del nuevo escenario en el que nos adentramos. El legendario hacker Charlie Miller ―exempleado de la agencia nacional de Inteligencia de Estados Unidos (la NSA) y conocido, entre otras cosas, por ser el primero en hackear los iPhones o por lograr controlar en 2014 el sistema de frenos, aceleración y dirección de un Jeep Grand Cherokee― tiene claro que esta tecnología nos ha colocado en otra pantalla. “¿Podemos, por favor, dejar de hablar sobre cómo nos matará la IA rebelde y volver a fijarnos en todas las vulnerabilidades geniales que está encontrando?”, dijo en la red social X hace apenas dos meses.
La IA lo cambia todo
Esa es la clave: la IA ha acelerado los tiempos, y eso equivale a cambiar el tablero de la partida de la ciberseguridad. Esta tecnología es una aliada formidable para quienes tratan de prevenir los ciberataques, pero también para quienes los diseñan y ejecutan. “La IA puede ayudar a identificar fallos de día cero [zero day, los que todavía no han sido descubiertos por nadie] y a desarrollar exploits [el programa que aprovecha un fallo o vulnerabilidad], todo ello rápidamente”, apunta Lukasz Olejnik, consultor de ciberseguridad e investigador en el Departamento de Estudios de Guerra del King’s College de Londres.
Los programas informáticos están escritos con miles de líneas de código que contienen instrucciones que el ordenador interpreta y ejecuta para realizar diferentes tareas. Los sistemas operativos, por ejemplo, pueden tener millones de líneas. Cuanto más complejo sea un software, más probable es que haya algún error en ese texto. Ese fallo es lo que en el sector llaman una vulnerabilidad. La razón de ser de las actualizaciones de software es parchear los fallos que se van encontrando, de modo que no puedan ser explotados por ciberdelincuentes.
La IA ha roto el equilibrio de este proceso. “Hemos entrado en una era en la que descubrir y explotar vulnerabilidades es mucho más rápido que solucionarlas”, dice Olejnik. Según datos recogidos por el fondo Andreessen Horowitz, el tiempo promedio que pasa entre que se divulga una vulnerabilidad y se lanza un ataque para explotarla era de 63 días en 2018. En 2025, se ataca una semana antes de divulgarse el fallo o bug.
“La IA puede ayudar a los atacantes a investigar objetivos, redactar mensajes convincentes, generar código y detectar vulnerabilidades en el software. Puede agilizar y abaratar algunas fases de una operación, lo que permite que un mismo actor intente más ataques. Es un cambio muy significativo, incluso aunque muchas de las técnicas de ataque ya sean conocidas”, señala el experto en ciberseguridad Mikko Hyppönen.
Cabe esperar, además, que esta progresión no se detenga. “Lo que más me preocupa es que se automatice todo el proceso. El hecho de que un programa busque puntos débiles en otro programa cambia la economía de los ataques. A medida que el coste disminuye, cada vez hay más objetivos por los que merece la pena esforzarse”, alerta Hyppönen.
De lo digital a lo físico
La aceleración y democratización de los ciberataques es solo una parte del dibujo. La ilustración se completa con otro elemento: la barrera que separa el mundo digital del físico se diluye. Se puede recuperar una base de datos si se ha guardado una copia de seguridad, pero no se puede recuperar comida estropeada. “Vivimos en un sistema ciberfísico, en el que los dispositivos físicos son controlados u operados remotamente por tecnologías de la información”, subraya Vladimir Dashchenko, investigador principal de la división de infraestructuras críticas e industriales de Kaspersky.
Volviendo a la semana pasada, un ciberataque elevó la temperatura de neveras y congeladores de supermercados de una docena de países europeos, echando a perder toneladas de comida. El ataque, idéntico a otro desarrollado tres semanas antes, se lanzó también sobre los refrigeradores del organismo que gestiona en Francia las donaciones de sangre, aunque en este caso se logró frenar.
No es la primera vez que un ciberataque impacta en el mundo real. En 2007, hace casi 20 años, el entonces vicepresidente de EE UU, Dick Cheney, dio orden de que se desactivara la función WiFi de su marcapasos. Un año después, investigadores de la Universidad de Massachusetts lograron hackear uno de esos dispositivos para detener a voluntad el sistema de bombeo. Fue un primer aviso.
Hubo más. En 2010, los servicios secretos de EE UU e Israel lograron introducir sendos pendrives en las centrales nucleares iraníes de Bushehr y Natanz. Por esa vía se descargó en sus sistemas Stuxnet, un gusano informático (un virus que se replica para infectar otros ordenadores) que dañó físicamente muchas centrifugadoras de uranio.
En 2014, un ciberataque provocó fallos en el sistema de una acería en Alemania que impidió apagar de forma controlada un alto horno, lo que causó “daños masivos”, según el BSI, la agencia de cibeserseguridad nacional del país. En 2015 y 2016, con la anexión de Crimea todavía reciente, Rusia lanzó uno de los ataques más sofisticados que se recuerdan contra infraestructuras energéticas. “BlackEnergy e Industroyer lograron colarse en los sistemas de control de subestaciones eléctricas ucranias. Los atacantes no necesitaron destruir equipos, ya que utilizaron las propias funciones de operación de la infraestructura para interrumpir el servicio y dejar sin electricidad a decenas de miles de personas en pleno invierno”, explica Josep Albors, responsable de investigación de ESET España.
Fue muy sonado también el ransomware (secuestro de sistemas) que sufrió en 2021 la compañía Colonial, lo que hizo que detuvieran de forma preventiva la actividad de uno de los mayores oleoductos de EE UU, provocando desabastecimiento en el país. El ataque se atribuye al grupo norcoreano Lazarus, que la semana pasada dio el mayor golpe cibernético de la historia, robando 6.300 millones de dólares en criptomonedas al portal Binance. Este verano, hackers vinculados a Irán atacaron 30 instalaciones hídricas de 12 Estados, provocando fallos de suministro de agua en algunas ciudades.
El incidente de las neveras no es un hecho aislado. Estas cosas ya pasaban. Pero ahora pasan más. “Aunque los ciberataques contra infraestructuras críticas llevan mucho tiempo produciéndose, la cantidad de los mismos se ha incrementado notablemente”, dice Albors.
La nueva normalidad
Hay ataques extremadamente complejos, que requieren meses de preparación, planificación y desarrollo de código. Es el caso de los primeros golpes a las infraestructuras, como Stuxnet, que logró retrasar algunos años el programa nuclear iraní, o BlackEnergy, que dejó sin calefacción a miles de ucranios en pleno invierno.
El de las neveras es más sencillo. Las primeras investigaciones apuntan al uso de contraseñas poco robustas o predeterminadas y la falta de actualización de equipos. Es una señal de los nuevos tiempos. “El ataque no parece muy sofisticado, y eso debería preocuparnos todavía más: no hace falta ser un actor potente para provocar problemas físicos importantes”, reflexiona Eusebio Nieva, director técnico de Check Point Software para España y Portugal. “Hoy hablamos de refrigeradores de supermercados, pero mañana podrían ser instalaciones sanitarias, industria, logística o transportes”, añade.
Cada vez hay más dispositivos conectados, así que la superficie de ataque no deja de crecer. “Ya no necesitas irrumpir en un supermercado para destruir la comida que haya allí. Lo que ha pasado esta semana es la confirmación práctica de la ‘Ley Hypponen’: si está conectado, es vulnerable”, dice Hypponen. La motivación de los atacantes tampoco está clara. “Algunos quieren dinero. Otros, espionaje. Los hay que buscan sembrar el caos. En las últimas semanas hemos visto de las tres, y las fronteras se solapan”, razona este informático finlandés. ¿Geopolítica? ¿Oportunismo? ¿Ánimo de lucro? Probablemente un poco de cada.
Lo que también está claro es que los ataques de hoy contra las infraestructuras físicas no solo son más frecuentes, sino también más peligrosos que los de hace una década. “Nuestros sistemas son frágiles, y contienen muchas deudas técnicas [el coste asociado a elegir soluciones de menor calidad en el desarrollo de software] que se han acumulado en las últimas décadas. Corregir eso llevará tiempo, y entre tanto nos arriesgamos a sufrir la cibertormenta perfecta”, señala Olejnik.

articles.title: Pendant le Black Friday 2026, l'aspirateur balai Dyson V8 Cyclone passe à 248,99 €
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 – L'aspirateur balai Dyson V8 Cyclone à 248,99 € (-11%)
L'aspirateur balai Dyson V8 Cyclone passe sous les 250 € chez Amazon soit une baisse d'environ 11% sur le prix habituellement constaté.
L'innovation peut-elle se nicher dans la réinterprétation ? Ce qui apparaît comme un sujet de bac de philo trouvera peut-être une réponse après notre test du Dyson V8 Cyclone, la vision 2025 d'un aspirateur-balai sorti en 2016.

Points forts
- Belles performances d'aspiration.
- Entretien facile.
- Relativement discret, aussi bien visuellement qu'acoustiquement.
Points faibles
- Autonomie trop faible à la puissance turbo.
- Extraction de la brosse pénible.
- Manque d'astuces pratiques (pas d'indicateur d'autonomie, de rampe de leds…).
Dans les grandes lignes, le Dyson V8 Cyclone reste le même que le V8 “normal”. Pour le meilleur et pour le pire, serait-on tenté d'ajouter. Certes, il existe quelques menues différences au niveau de la prise en main, une amélioration de la gestion du bruit, et on ne peut que féliciter Dyson d'avoir enfin pris le virage de la batterie amovible. On regrette d'autant plus que cet aspirateur-balai n'ait pas pris celui de l'indicateur d'autonomie précis, ou encore de la rampe de leds sur la tête d'aspiration. Ceci étant, malgré une durée de vie en mode turbo famélique, le V8 Cyclone est un modèle efficace et très simple à entretenir.

articles.title: Asteroide misterioso acelera no espaço e desafia explicações científicas
articles.text:
Um pequeno objeto espacial identificado como 1998 KY26 está apresentando uma aceleração incomum, que ainda não tem uma explicação definitiva. Uma das hipóteses consideradas pelos cientistas é que ele seja um cometa escuro, mas um novo estudo publicado na revista Icarus coloca essa possibilidade em dúvida.
A pesquisa foi conduzida pelos engenheiros aeroespaciais Korbin Hansen e Masatoshi Hirabayashi, do Instituto de Tecnologia da Geórgia. Segundo os pesquisadores, o asteroide, que tem aproximadamente 11 metros de diâmetro, apresenta temperaturas elevadas demais para conservar o gelo necessário à liberação de gases que poderia explicar seu movimento incomum.
Por que o asteroide está acelerando?
Em geral, asteroides seguem trajetórias influenciadas por forças conhecidas, como a gravidade e a pressão da radiação solar. O 1998 KY26, no entanto, apresenta um comportamento diferente: sua trajetória registra uma aceleração incomum, perpendicular ao plano de sua órbita.
Uma das explicações levantadas é que o objeto seja, na verdade, um cometa escuro. Diferentemente dos cometas tradicionais, que costumam apresentar caudas brilhantes e visíveis, esses corpos podem liberar gases sem produzir sinais aparentes dessa atividade.
Nos cometas, o gelo presente na composição do objeto passa por um processo chamado sublimação, no qual se transforma diretamente em gás. Quando esse material escapa para o espaço, pode produzir um impulso adicional, alterando o movimento do corpo celeste.
O 1998 KY26 também chama a atenção por sua rotação rápida: ele completa uma volta em apenas 5,35 minutos. Essas características levaram cientistas a considerar a possibilidade de que o objeto pertença à categoria dos cometas escuros.
Temperatura coloca hipótese dos cometas escuros em dúvida
Para investigar essa possibilidade, Hansen e Hirabayashi desenvolveram um modelo que considera informações conhecidas sobre o objeto, incluindo tamanho, órbita, refletividade e composição provável. Com esses dados, calcularam as temperaturas em diferentes regiões da superfície e do interior do corpo celeste.
A análise apontou um problema para a hipótese. Para que o gelo de água enterrado sobreviva por longos períodos, a temperatura precisa permanecer abaixo de aproximadamente 145 kelvins, equivalente a -128 °C.
Entretanto, mesmo as regiões mais frias do 1998 KY26 apresentam temperatura média de pelo menos 212 kelvins (-61 °C) ao longo de sua órbita ao redor do Sol. Esse nível de calor seria suficiente para impedir a conservação prolongada do gelo.
Os pesquisadores também calcularam que, mesmo se a água congelada representasse 1% da massa do asteroide, todo esse material desapareceria em pouco mais de 2 mil anos. Caso o gelo fosse responsável pela aceleração observada, ele se esgotaria em apenas 62 anos.
O estudo, portanto, enfraquece a explicação de que a atividade cometária esteja impulsionando o objeto. Ainda assim, os cientistas não descartam completamente a presença de gelo, já que não se sabe há quanto tempo o 1998 KY26 ocupa sua órbita atual.
Missão japonesa pode ajudar a resolver o mistério
Outra possibilidade considerada pelos pesquisadores é a pressão da radiação solar. A luz emitida pelo Sol exerce uma força sobre os objetos espaciais. Embora pequena, ela poderia ser suficiente para explicar a aceleração observada no asteroide.
Uma investigação mais detalhada pode acontecer nos próximos anos. A espaçonave Hayabusa2, da agência espacial japonesa, está a caminho do 1998 KY26, com encontro previsto para julho de 2031.
A missão poderá fornecer informações mais precisas sobre as características do objeto e ajudar a esclarecer a origem de seu comportamento incomum.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: Brava Security Emerges From Stealth With $15 Million in Funding
articles.text:
Security operations startup Brava Security has emerged from stealth mode with $15 million in a seed funding round led by F2 Venture Capital and Pitango VC, with support from several angel investors.
Tel Aviv-based Brava was founded in 2024 by Israeli intelligence alumni Idan Basre, who serves as CEO, and Itay Gabbay, the company’s CTO.
Brava has built an AI-powered platform that focuses on modeling attacker behavior, simulating attacks to analyze generated telemetry for security gaps.
Using business context, the solution shows how an attack would manifest in customers’ environments, reveals what defenses could miss, and rewrites SIEM detections, while allowing security teams to investigate further.
“The hard part of security was never writing detections. It’s knowing exactly what an attack will look like in a specific environment, across all of its log sources, before it ever happens. That’s the problem our models were built to solve,” said Gabbay.
Brava says this approach closes an important gap in modern security defenses, since AI agents typically cannot investigate attacks their systems haven’t detected.
“You can’t automate a decision based on evidence no one ever proved. We’re solving the problem that comes before AI can make the right decision: making sure the security infrastructure actually sees the threats it’s supposed to detect,” Basre said.
According to Brava, its platform can provide initial insights within 10-15 minutes of onboarding. The solution integrates with more than 70 sources and destinations and does not require changes to existing security infrastructure.
The startup will use the fresh funding to accelerate product development and market expansion. It currently has an R&D team in Israel and a commercial team in the US.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Regensburg. Original written by Karoline Stürmer. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S. Maier, R. Spachtholz, K. Glöckl, C. M. Bustamante, S. Lingl, M. Maczejka, J. Schön, A. Riedel, K. Richter, F. J. Giessibl, F. P. Bonafé, M. A. Huber, A. Rubio, J. Repp, R. Huber. Tracking electrons at the space-time limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (8): 961 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01932-0

articles.title: En una isla de California solo quedaban 15 zorros a finales de los noventa: tras expulsar a las águilas reales, hoy son más de 300
articles.text:
En la década de los 90, las Islas del Canal frente a la costa de California fueron el escenario de una catástrofe ecológica fulminante. En este punto, el zorro isleño, un carnívoro endémico y rey indiscutible de este archipiélago, empezó a desaparecer a un ritmo bastante alto. Y es que las cifras no dejaban lugar a dudas, puesto que en su punto más bajo, la isla de Santa Rosa pasó de tener 1.780 ejemplares a apenas 15, mientras que la de Santa Cruz vio cómo su población se desplomaba de 1.400 a tan solo 55.
En peligro. Estas cifras, en un periodo muy corto de tiempo hacía activar todas las alarmas, puesto que estaban literalmente a un paso de la extinción. El problema es que los investigadores tardaron demasiado en ver que el culpable no estaba en el cambio climático o en una enfermedad que se estaba propagando, sino en un extraño efecto dominó provocado por el humano.
El mecanismo. La pregunta era clara: ¿cómo desaparecen miles de zorros en apenas años? Y la respuesta la tuvo un investigador que a principios de los 2000 apuntó a que el responsable estaba en un fenómeno conocido como 'hiperdepredación mediada por cerdos'.
Aunque parezca raro, tiene sentido, puesto que durante décadas, los ganaderos habían ido llevando cerdos a estas islas, los cuales terminaron asilvestrándose y multiplicándose sin control. El problema es que tanta cantidad de alimento en las islas atrajo desde el continente a un depredador formidable que nunca antes había aparecido por el archipiélago: el águila real.
El depredador. Las águilas reales se instalaron en las islas para cazar cerdos, pero pronto descubrieron al zorro isleño que también rondaba por esas tierras. Los zorros, al haber evolucionado en un entorno donde no se tenían que preocupar por ningún depredador que viniera del cielo, no desarrollaron mecanismos de evasión, por lo que eran presas muy fáciles para las águilas. Y fue aquí cuando comenzó la masacre doble.
Un plan de choque. Con la especie al borde del abismo, las autoridades tuvieron que tomar medidas. La primera de ellas debía pasar por sacar a las águilas reales, organizando expediciones en las que se capturaron y reubicaron fuera del archipiélago a 44 águilas, algo que hizo que el zorro comenzara a recuperarse.
Pero además de esto, se comenzó una guerra contra los cerdos con un programa de erradicación que costó unos cinco millones de dólares. Con este se logró en más o menos 400 días eliminar a 5.036 cerdos. De esta manera, las islas dejaban de ser un bufet libre para las águilas reales.
Para prevenir. Con el objetivo de que esto no pasara más, y que las águilas reales no volvieran a por los zorros, se introdujo a su competidor natural, que es el pigargo americano. Estas águilas se alimentan de peces y aves marinas y son muy territoriales, por lo que su mera presencia hacía casi imposible que las águilas reales se atrevieran a acercarse.
La recuperación. El éxito fue tan importante que las autoridades anunciaron que el zorro isleño representaba la recuperación más rápida que ha visto en un mamífero que estaba en peligro de extinción. Y la verdad es que la recuperación ha sido muy positiva, puesto que a día de hoy en la isla de Santa Cruz se han contabilizado 3.086 zorros, mientras que en San Miguel la población es de 322 individuos.

articles.title: US officials say a Chinese businesswoman close to Nvidia's Jensen Huang was a spy for Beijing
articles.text:
The spy who shagged? US intelligence believes Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who befriended Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang while her company bought billions of dollars' worth of his AI chips, was spying for China's Ministry of State Security. Last spring, a memo that circulated among top Trump's policymakers said she had been recruited to learn about American AI chips and possibly influence the Nvidia chief to push for China to get the company's most advanced processors.
Jensen Huang is a close Trump ally and the Republican leaders of three House committees have now asked him to explain his dealings with his namesake in a closed-door briefing later this month.
US export rules keep Nvidia's best chips out of China, and he has spent years pushing Washington to let the company sell more of its technology in the country.
US intelligence agencies had kept Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, under electronic surveillance for at least a year. The report also stated that President Trump was briefed on the relationship last year but chose not to act. The two Huangs are not related.
Her company, Megaspeed, began buying chips in 2024, around the time she and Jensen Huang were photographed together at a bar in Taipei. Many in the industry were surprised because the company had no visible track record in the field.
Megaspeed has been building data centers in Southeast Asia and renting their computing capacity to Alibaba. Nvidia can't ship its top data center chips to China, but renting offshore capacity lets a Chinese company run workloads on that same hardware without importing it. The setup effectively allows Chinese companies to access computing power that they cannot import directly under US export controls.
Alice Huang belonged to a cluster of companies and investors based around Shanghai and Zhejiang Province. That group used its connections with Shanghai officials to move from mobile video games into data centers. It also has a financial tie to China's defense sector through an investment in a cybersecurity subsidiary of China Electronics Technology Group, a major military technology maker.
People who have met her say she speaks fluent English and attends industry conferences and private executive dinners. Besides Jensen Huang, she knows the leaders of Gigabyte, a major assembler of Nvidia-based supercomputers.
Peter Mattis, a former CIA counterintelligence analyst who now leads the Jamestown Foundation, said the ministry sees technology as "the key fight for dominance in the economic world."
 – Patrick Moorhead (@PatrickMoorhead) November 7, 2026
"They're interested in what's taking place in technology, in the technical specifications of what's being built and in shaping decision-making as it relates to those things," Mattis told the New York Times. "Jensen is someone you'd want to influence because he wields a lot of power and is at the crux of a world-shaping technology."
Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo said the company does not share classified information with customers. He also said customers do not ask Nvidia to press Washington to change its chip policy on China. He said Beijing had "consistently promoted its own domestic alternatives in China, including Huawei, and strictly limited imports of our data center products."
Rizzo has described Jensen Huang's meetings with Alice Huang as "not unusual," noting that the CEO speaks with thousands of executives who do business with Nvidia each year.
Liu Chang, a spokesman for the Chinese embassy, called the reporting "unsubstantiated" and "nothing but smears against China." Alice Huang did not respond to repeated requests for comment. The White House and the CIA declined to comment.
Jensen Huang argues that selling in China would let Nvidia compete with Huawei and slow its progress. In 2025 he persuaded Trump to reverse a ban and allow sales of a less capable Nvidia chip. The two later agreed to let Nvidia sell its second-most-powerful chip in China, with the US government taking 25% of the revenue. Trump also considered approving Blackwell, Nvidia's newest architecture, but dropped the idea.
At an investor conference in May, Jensen Huang said China should not get Blackwell or the upcoming Rubin chip. He said the United States should have "the first, the most and the best, but simultaneously all American companies should compete globally."
The Ministry of State Security was founded in 1983 and spent years behind the People's Liberation Army's spy and hacking units in Beijing's pecking order. That began to change after Xi Jinping took power in 2012 and put money into the ministry. It took on more of China's espionage work after a 2015 US-China agreement to rein in cyber operations. The Justice Department later accused hackers linked to the ministry of trying to steal US technology.
By 2023, the ministry had become a rival to the CIA and was using AI to pick and profile targets. It is estimated to have hundreds of thousands of agents, far more than the United States has counterintelligence officers. China aims to lead the world in AI by 2030.
The ministry's current head, Chen Yixin, is from Zhejiang and served under Xi when the now-president ran the province in the early 2000s. In a September essay in the state-run magazine China Cyberspace, Chen said China needed to assert control over AI, and that algorithms would help countries "gain the initiative on the battlefield."

articles.title: „Nichts mehr, was KI nicht kann“: Hat das Mathe-Studium noch Zukunft?
articles.text:
Mathe-Professor kapituliert: Warum Hausaufgaben durch KI sinnlos sind
KI hat die Art und Weise, wie junge Menschen studieren, grundlegend verändert und zwingt auch Professor:innen zum Umdenken. Richard Borcherds von der UC Berkeley sieht beispielsweise keinen Sinn mehr darin, die Hausaufgaben seiner Kursteilnehmer:innen zu benoten. Der Einsatz von KI sei unvermeidbar geworden. Es sei daher sinnlos, Lehrkräfte dafür zu bezahlen, die Hausarbeiten der Student:innen auf ihre Richtigkeit zu prüfen.
Wandel der universitären Lernkultur durch KI
Im vergangenen Jahr ergab eine OpenAI-Analyse, dass in den USA College-Student:innen ChatGPT häufiger nutzen als jede andere Zielgruppe. „Sie treffen keine wichtigen Lebensentscheidungen mehr, ohne vorher ChatGPT um Rat zu fragen, was sie tun sollen”, erklärte CEO Sam Altman Mitte 2025 auf einem Event. Viele setzen KI ein, um Zeit zu sparen. Einige Student:innen fügen sogar gezielt Tippfehler hinzu oder verwenden „dumme” Prompts, damit ihre Texte natürlicher klingen und nicht auffallen. In Deutschland ist KI im Studium ebenfalls weit verbreitet. Laut einer bundesweiten Befragung der Hochschule Darmstadt nutzen 92 Prozent der Befragten Tools wie ChatGPT zumindest gelegentlich. Die häufigsten Anwendungsfälle sind demnach das Klären von Verständnisfragen sowie das Erstellen, Analysieren und Übersetzen von Texten.
Borcherds beobachtet eigenen Angaben zufolge schon länger, dass viele seiner Student:innen KI nutzen, um ihre Hausaufgaben zu erledigen und regelmäßig Bestnoten zu erzielen. Zudem gab OpenAI kürzlich bekannt, mit seinen KI-Modellen eine ganze Reihe mathematischer Probleme gelöst zu haben, darunter das sogenannte Navier-Stokes-Existenz- und Glattheitsproblem. Daraufhin sei Borcherds zu dem Schluss gekommen, dass eine Benotung von Matheaufgaben im KI-Zeitalter sinnlos sei. „Wenn sich die KI weiterhin im derzeitigen Tempo verbessert, wird es in wenigen Jahren nichts mehr geben, was menschliche Mathematiker:innen tun können, was die KI nicht besser kann“, so Borcherds im Interview mit The Daily Californian.
Unzuverlässigkeit technischer KI-Detektionssysteme in der Plagiatsprüfung
Derzeit bewertet der Professor die Hausaufgaben nur noch danach, ob sie vollständig abgegeben wurden. Er räumte ein, dass dies „kein besonders gutes System“ sei, aber im Moment habe er keine Alternative. Die Universität wies die Lehrkräfte an, in die Kurserwartungen eine Erklärung zum Einsatz von KI-Tools für Kursarbeiten aufzunehmen. Je nach Thema und Kursniveau könne diese variieren. Der Campus testete zudem mehrere KI-Detektoren, darunter Turnitin und Rumi, kam aber zu dem Ergebnis, dass sie sich nicht für einen standardisierten Einsatz eignen. Das Beispiel einer australischen Universität zeigt, dass solche Tools nicht immer richtig liegen: Ihr KI-Detektor soll im Jahr 2024 fast 6.000 Fälle mutmaßlichen Fehlverhaltens im Zusammenhang mit KI registriert haben – 90 Prozent davon hätten sich allerdings als Fehlalarm herausgestellt.
Zukunftsperspektiven für mathematische Studiengänge angesichts der Automatisierung
Damit stellt sich auch die Frage, wie relevant Studienfächer wie Mathematik noch sind, wenn KI jedes Problem lösen kann. Borcherds wisse selbst nicht mehr, ob er junge Menschen noch dazu ermutigen solle, Mathematik zu studieren. Dabei hätte der Beruf angesichts des KI-Booms vor fünf Jahren noch als einer der sichersten gegolten. „Ich habe keine Ahnung, was ich raten soll. Ich habe sogar ChatGPT genau diese Frage gestellt, und selbst ChatGPT sagte, es habe keine Ahnung, was passieren werde“, so der Professor. Die 722 von OpenAI veröffentlichten Fachartikel haben in der wissenschaftlichen Gemeinschaft insgesamt große Unruhe ausgelöst. Die neu gegründete Association for Human Mathematics wolle sich jetzt dafür einsetzen, „die Mathematik als menschliches Unterfangen vor der Bedrohung durch Künstliche Intelligenz“ zu schützen.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 26.10.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.

articles.title: Iris Ohyama data cloud breach exposes info of 7.7 million customers
articles.text:
Japanese manufacturer Iris Ohyama, the operator of the Iris Plaza shopping platform, disclosed that personal information belonging to about 7.7 million people may have been exposed after unauthorized access to a third-party cloud service the company used.
The company discovered the incident late last month and publicly disclosed it with limited details, along with an announcement that the site would be temporarily suspended.
In an update earlier this week, the company said it had discovered a suspicious file in an external cloud service used by the Iris Plaza online store.
“We immediately suspended Iris Plaza and related systems and began an investigation. We confirmed unauthorized access by a third party and disclosed it in our first notice on October 29,” [machine translated] the company said.
The investigation has confirmed that customer data stored in the compromised external cloud service may have been accessed by unauthorized actors.
While the company is still trying to determine the number of records exposed and how many people are impacted, it notes that the impact extends to up to 5.8 million registered members and former members, and 1.9 million non-members.
Iris Plaza is the online storefront for the Iris Ohyama Group, a major Japanese manufacturer of household products ranging from storage units and LED lighting to home appliances and garden accessories.
According to the company's notification, the following information may have been exposed:
- Full names
- Physical addresses
- Phone numbers
- Email addresses
- Gender
- Dates of birth
- Account passwords
The exposed data types vary per individual. For example, no passwords are stored for former members.
Iris Plaza said it stores passwords for active registered members in encrypted form, though it did not specify which encryption scheme it uses.
The company also said that credit card information was not stored in the affected cloud service.
As of November 5, Iris Plaza had received no reports of misuse of the exposed information or financial loss tied to the incident.
In response to the incident, the company’s online store (SIMPLE STYLE) and related systems were suspended on October 28.
The same applies to websites for Iris Tech Service Co., Ltd. services, including home appliance subscriptions and furniture and appliance delivery and installation.
Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission and police were notified on October 29, 2026.
BleepingComputer has contacted Iris Plaza to learn more about the attack and whether a ransom payment has been demanded. A spokesperson told us that they received no direct communications from the attacker and have not identified the perpetrators.

articles.title: Le poids de GTA 6, les Xiaomi 18 Pro en France, un VPN gratuit et Ocarina of Time — Frandroid
articles.text:
Pour savoir avant tout le monde quand GTA 6 se débloque sur votre console ou quand un nouveau smartphone arrive en France, le plus simple est encore de nous suivre sur Google. Pour ne rien rater de l’actu, suivez-nous sur Google et Google News.
GTA 6 : libérez 212 Go avant le 10 novembre
Rockstar a publié son calendrier, et le pré-chargement de GTA 6 ouvrira le 10 novembre sur PS5 et Xbox Series X|S, neuf jours avant la sortie du 19 novembre. Le jeu pèse jusqu’à 212 Go selon la console, soit plus de la moitié du stockage d’une Xbox Series S. Les horaires d’ouverture ne sont pas les mêmes sur PlayStation et sur Xbox, et ceux qui achètent la version boîte (79,99 euros en édition Standard) n’y échapperont pas non plus, puisqu’elle contient un simple code de téléchargement. Retrouvez notre dossier complet sur tout ce qu’il y a à savoir sur GTA 6 (date, précommandes, disponibilité…).
À noter que Rockstar a encore publier 39 nouvelles images du jeu pour vous plonger dans Vice City et l’État de Leonida.
    À lire aussi : 
Quelle console choisir pour jouer à GTA 6 à sa sortie ?
Les Xiaomi 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max arrivent en France dès ce mois-ci
Xiaomi l’a confirmé sur X : la série 18 Pro sort à l’international en novembre. Ce sont les premiers smartphones de la marque avec écran secondaire à arriver en Europe, les 17 Pro n’ayant jamais quitté la Chine, et nous avons déjà pu tester le 18 Pro grâce à un modèle rapporté de là-bas. Le SoC Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 de Qualcomm est au programme, en version Extreme sur le Pro Max. Les fuites de billbil-kun évoquent des prix de 1 399 à 1 799 euros, avec des batteries plus petites que sur les modèles chinois, d’après la fiche d’un revendeur italien. Rappel que nous avons déjà testé le modèle chinois du Xiaomi 18 Pro.
La taxe sur le gigaoctet finalement abandonnée… pour le moment
Adoptée le 30 octobre 2026 par 11 voix contre 10, dans un hémicycle quasi vide, la taxe sur le gigaoctet était un amendement du député socialiste Laurent Lhardit au budget 2027. Elle visait à faire payer 5,5 centimes par gigaoctet envoyé aux internautes français aux plateformes comme Netflix, Google ou Amazon, pour un rendement espéré de 10 milliards d’euros par an. Faute d’exemption, elle aurait aussi frappé des acteurs non lucratifs comme VideoLAN, l’éditeur de VLC, et aurait sans doute fini par se répercuter sur les abonnements et les annonceurs, d’où une levée de boucliers dans le secteur, de Xavier Niel à VideoLAN. Elle n’aura pas survécu une semaine : le 4 novembre, les députés ont rejeté toute la partie « recettes » du budget, par 458 voix contre et aucune pour, emportant avec elle tous les amendements votés, dont cette taxe. Le Sénat examinera à partir du 20 novembre le texte initial du gouvernement, qui ne la contient pas, même si rien n’empêche l’idée de revenir sous une autre forme.
Avast lance un VPN gratuit sans plafond de données ni publicité
Aucune carte bancaire, aucune limite de données et autant d’appareils que vous le souhaitez : Avast VPN est disponible gratuitement en France depuis le 4 novembre. Le changement de cap est net, puisque l’éditeur tchèque ne proposait jusqu’ici qu’un essai de 60 jours pour SecureLine, ou un VPN bridé à 5 Go par semaine dans Avast One. Sur le papier, la technique tient la route avec le protocole WireGuard, un kill switch et une protection contre les fuites DNS. Une offre aussi généreuse pose forcément la question de la contrepartie, et nous avons regardé ce qu’elle cache.
Le remake d’Ocarina of Time tournerait sur le moteur de Tears of the Kingdom
Nintendo n’a rien dit du socle technique de son remake de Zelda : Ocarina of Time, sorti le 5 novembre sur Switch 2. articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.
